Hence it came about afterwards that the Bacchantes, celebrating his ceremonies, handled serpents without feeling any harm from them, as Plutarch writes in the life of Alexander, where he speaks of Olympias his mother, to whom it seemed that she had been made pregnant by a serpent; which was believed also by the mother of Scipio, as the same Plutarch reports, because a great snake was often seen entering her room.
Young bull torn apart in the ceremonies of Bacchus

Catullus had in mind that ceremony of handling serpents of which I spoke when he said of the ministers and followers of Bacchus that some girded themselves with serpents; just as he showed another mysterious ceremony too, saying that some carried the limbs of the torn young bull. For it is read that Pentheus, king of Thebes, was a despiser of Bacchus and of his ceremonies, and would not have them celebrated in any way. Bacchus took such vengeance for this that he made Pentheus appear to his mother and to the other women who were celebrating the Bacchanalian feasts as a young bull, or a boar, as Ovid says, that had come to disturb the sacred ceremonies; whereupon all of them were at once around him and tore him to pieces, which they then carried in their hands while they went furiously running about, glad of the vengeance; and in memory of this the Bacchantes at times, at the feasts of their god, used to tear a calf apart, and each of them carried off one of the torn limbs.
Osiris
Tibullus

Of this it could perhaps be said that it was done to represent what the fables relate that Typhon did with the companions of Osiris, because Osiris was in Egypt what Bacchus was among the Greeks; hence Tibullus attributes to him all that we have already said of Bacchus, and describes him thus, saying:

lines: The first who ever made the plough
was Osiris, and the first who showed
how the earth was to be cultivated.
And how it was then to be sown
he showed also, and when sweet fruits
a man might find on the unknown tree.
From him all the others learned
to wed the weak vine
to the stake, so that it might bear better afterwards,
and to cut those branches by which
the plant's strength to produce
the grapes so welcome to mortals is hindered.
For from these, ripe in their season,
the rough feet squeeze out the sweet juice,
as the same Osiris taught to do.
blocks.author: Tibullus

blocks.text: And after, some verses later, he goes on thus:

lines: In you, Osiris, no sign is ever seen
of sadness, and from you always stay far
the sad thoughts, the weeping and the sighs.
But a fair chorus singing in joyful measures
accompanies you ever wherever you go,
so that love, play and laughter are always with you.
You are adorned with fair flowers, and your brow
is girt with ivy, and a golden robe
that reaches the ground you drag behind you.
Sometimes a purple one is given you too,
and with sweet sound there accompanies you
the hollow pipe and the basket crammed
with mysteries that are always hidden.
blocks.author: Tibullus

blocks.text: Osiris in the form of a hawk

The Egyptians sometimes depicted this Osiris in the form of a hawk, a bird that sees very well and flies swiftest of all, as the Sun does too, of which he was the image. Hence more often still they depicted him, again in Egypt, as Plutarch writes, in the form of a man who has the natural member erect and a red cloth around him. The reason for this I shall give a little further on, when I take up Priapus, who was a part and member of Osiris.
Osiris killed and torn apart

For it is read of him that Typhon his brother, having formed a conspiracy of many against him, killed him, and having cut him into many pieces distributed them all among the conspirators, except the virile member, which none of them wanted, and which was therefore thrown into the Nile, which carried it away. Isis his wife, grieved at the loss of her husband, of whom she did not know what had become, and whom she had been seeking for a good while, as soon as she learned this, went against Typhon and defeated him, and recovered from the conspirators the limbs that they had divided among themselves, which she put all together in order, and not finding among them the one that had been thrown into the Nile, she was extremely sorry for it, and ordered that in future his image should be revered and worshipped with many ceremonies, as it always was afterwards under the name of Priapus.
Ceremonies of Osiris
Lucan

And in memory of all this she ordered also that every year at a certain time, with solemn ceremony, weeping and lamenting, men should go seeking Osiris, and soon after should hold a feast with great gladness, carrying about with solemnity a beautiful boy who represented Osiris already found. Hence, because this ceremony was renewed every year, Lucan said of him that he was never sought enough.
Horus

Almost the same happened with Horus: Isis his mother mourned him for a while, thinking she had lost him, but then found him and was very glad. By him, who was likewise worshipped in Egypt, some, such as Macrobius, have held that the Sun is to be understood, and that from him the Hours (*Hore*), those small parts of time that measure the day, were named. Others have understood the world by him. His idol was that of a youth who held with one hand the shameful parts of Typhon, because it is read that he defeated him; he did not kill him, but he rendered vain all his power, though Typhon, changed into a crocodile, fled from him. Hence there was a law in Apollinopolis, a city of Egypt, which commanded that no regard be had for crocodiles, but that everyone should hunt them and kill as many as he could, and all those that were caught and killed were placed before the temple of Horus.
Typhon
Plato

Of Typhon the fables feigned, as Apollodorus recounts, that he was begotten by the Earth in vengeance for the Giants once killed by the gods of Heaven. He was of two natures, human and bestial. Hence Plato too in the *Phaedrus* calls him a beast of many natures, burning and furious; and he surpassed in size of body and in strength all that were ever born of the earth.

The upper part was in the form of a man, all covered with feathers, so great and so tall that it went above all the highest mountains and often touched the stars with its head; and stretching out his arms he reached with one hand to the West and with the other to the East, and from the one and the other came a hundred serpents, which held their heads forward. The legs were serpents, and there were others around them, which went winding up over the terrible body until they reached the high head, which was covered with horrid and filthy locks that hung down over the neck and shoulders; and such was the beard too, which descended from the great chin over the broad chest; the eyes were terrible and sparkled as if they were of fire, and the wide mouth likewise poured forth most burning flames.

The heavenly gods had such fear of him, when he turned against them, throwing fiery stones towards Heaven, that they fled into Egypt, and did not hold themselves safe even here before they were changed into various animals, as I have already said of many of them in the images drawn so far. But in the end he was defeated by Jupiter, according to Apollodorus, or, as others have held, as I said a little above, by Horus, who, though he had a different name, was nevertheless the same as Osiris. Hence in Hermopolis, a city of Egypt, they depicted the hippopotamus with a hawk fighting it while standing on it, and by the former they meant Typhon, image of all the evil that comes from the earth, and by this the virtue that resists him and renders vain all his furious onset, shown through Osiris, or Horus, who are therefore the Sun, just as for other reasons they were Bacchus; and as it was said in Egypt of Osiris that Typhon cut him into pieces, so the Greeks said that the Titans did the same to Bacchus.

Images of Typhon, brother of Osiris, and of Horus, son of Osiris, who is Bacchus among the Greeks, which Horus defeated the said Typhon, though changed into a crocodile; with the hippopotamus and the hawk, hieroglyphs denoting Virtue, which fights evil, resists it, and in the end defeats and tramples it.
Bacchus torn apart

This, as I said, perhaps the Bacchantes represented with the limbs of the torn calf. But that Bacchus was killed by the Titans, cut in pieces and cooked, and afterwards put together again and smeared with plaster, so that he might no longer be recognised, as Suda reports, signifies that the grapes are trodden and all broken by the peasants who press the wine from them, which boils, purging itself, in the great vessels, not only of wood but of stone also, and at times of plaster, and seems almost to be cooked; and some do cook it, as though it would keep better that way afterwards; and afterwards the torn limbs are put together again, because the vine in its season produces the grapes whole again.
Bacchus with the Eleusinian goddesses

Moreover, because Bacchus was believed also by some of the ancients to be that hidden power which gives all plants the strength to produce ripe fruits, Herodotus writes that he was a numen familiar to the Eleusinian goddesses, and went often with them. These were, as I said already, Ceres and Proserpina, who were believed to make the scattered seed germinate. And it is read in Pausanias also that the Athenians had in the temple of Ceres, among the other idols, that of Bacchus too, which held out a burning torch in its hand.
Porphyry

Hence Porphyry said, according to Eusebius, that Bacchus was represented with horns and dressed as a woman, to show that in plants both powers are present, of male and of female; and although it is read of the palm that it has both, and that it bears badly unless both are close together, nevertheless it is seen that in general every plant produces leaves and fruits by itself, without any other joining it, which is not so with animals, because these cannot generate unless the male and the female join together.

Hence perhaps the fables feigned that Priapus was born of Bacchus, to show the whole seminal power, which takes its strength from the Sun, in plants as in the other things produced by the earth. This was understood also in the image of Osiris that I drew a little above, the red cloth that he had around him showing that celestial heat which gives strength to the seed down to the bowels of the earth.
Suda
Priapus

And Suda writes that Priapus is the same as Bacchus, who in Egypt was called Horus, whose image was in the form of a youth who holds a sceptre in his right hand, as if he were lord of all that is born in this world of ours, and in the left the natural member, erect and extended, because the hidden seminal power comes from him; he has wings, to show how swift he is, and beside him is the disc. This was a broad, flat, round thing made of stone or metal, with which the ancients exercised themselves by throwing it up high, and here it showed the roundness of the universe, because the Sun, which is understood by Horus, encircles the world through the three that I mentioned [?].
qm: "per gli tre, ch'io dissi": it is not clear which "three" are meant; no three things through which the Sun encircles the world have been named earlier in this passage. Rendered literally.

blocks.text: Image of Horus, god of the Egyptians, who is Priapus and also Bacchus, understood as the seminal power and as the Sun; with the drawing of the disc signifying the roundness of the world, which is illuminated by the Sun and into which the Sun pours its power.
Ceremonies of the Bacchanalia
Phallophori

To show how alike Bacchus and Priapus were, or perhaps even one and the same thing, the ancients at the feasts of the Bacchanalia used to carry round the neck the figure of the virile member made of fig wood, and called by them Phallus, which they made afterwards of red leather also, as Suda reports; and having fastened it in front between their thighs, they went leaping with it in honour of Bacchus, and were then called Phallophori. They also covered their faces with very thin bark of trees, or with some skin, and wreathed their heads with ivy or violets.
Herodotus
Priapus

Herodotus writes that instead of this the Egyptians devised making some little statues, only a cubit long, with the natural member extended and almost greater than the whole body, which the women carried about at certain times through the villages, on certain little carts made on purpose for this, with pipes in front, singing in honour of Bacchus. And the Roman women afterwards did the same, carrying this member about with solemn pomp, and many ceremonies were ordained for it, which I pass over for worthy reasons; besides, they are of no use in drawing the image of Priapus. He was depicted as a boy, stout, ugly and ill-made, with the virile sign as large as all the rest of the body, like the little statues I have just spoken of, as Suda also describes him. Suda says that Juno, by touching Venus's belly, caused him to be born so, out of spite against Jupiter her husband, who had made Venus pregnant; although it is read also that Bacchus was the father of Priapus, as I have said above, and as Theodoret reports, who gives the reason for it by saying that by Venus wanton pleasure is understood, and by Bacchus the heat of wine drunk without measure, and that when these different things join together, Priapus is born of them, because he who lay down before rises thus and makes himself seen, and perhaps it was not known that he was there.
The god Mutinus
Varro
Lactantius
Saint Augustine

Like him, or rather the same, was the god Mutinus, who, seated, likewise showed a great member; and the new brides, before coupling with the husband, went to sit on his lap with solemn ceremony, wishing to show in that way that they gave him the first flower of their virginity, as Varro wrote, and Lactantius and Saint Augustine in the *City of God* have reported.
God of gardens
Tibullus

Priapus was also called by the ancients the god of gardens, and was therefore depicted in the form of a man with a beard and tousled hair, quite naked, and with a curved sickle in his right hand, as Tibullus describes him, pretending to ask him how it is that handsome youths love him, not at all handsome or adorned; and he speaks thus, in verses drawn into our language.

lines: O if you, kind Priapus [?], could have
shady roofs, so that neither snow nor Sun
might ever come to touch your bare head!
Tell me with what art you bring it about
that every handsome youth wishes you so much good,
and as best he can reveres and honours you?
You are not handsome, and full of squalor
are your uncombed locks, and your beard is tousled.
Where then does it come from, that everyone loves you?
You go naked as in the frozen season
of cold winter, so in the Sun
of the scorched, glowing summer.
All these were my words,
and he answered me with the sickle in hand,
the rustic offspring of Bacchus, thus.
blocks.author: Tibullus
qm: "Deh se tu possi hauer a'mo Priapo": "a'mo" is obscure; perhaps "almo" (kind, nourishing), which is how I have taken it, or an abbreviated word of address. The sense of the verse (wishing Priapus shady roofs) is not affected.

blocks.text: Image of Priapus, god of gardens, and of the virile member, and of the ass and the goat, sacred to him, since he is understood as the seminal or generative power. He is a god who punishes thieves and theft, which is signified in the sickle, and the animals are a sign of powerful generation.
Horace

They dressed him sometimes also in a cloth, which he held gathered with his hand, and carried fruits of every sort in the lap. And they made wreaths for him of everything that grew in the gardens, at the guard of which he stood with a long reed on his head to frighten the birds, and threatened with the big member that he held in his hand whoever should go to steal any of the things guarded by him. Hence, when Horace wishes to describe him, Priapus speaks of himself thus:

lines: I was a fig trunk, good for nothing,
when the carpenter got me,
and he was long in doubt what to do.
Not knowing what to make of me, and now wishing
to see a bench made of me, he thought
that to make a Priapus would be far better.
On this he resolved, and bestowed
his work on it, and I became a god,
an immense terror to thieves and birds.
For, having armed my right hand
with a curved sickle, I give thieves great fright,
and with the member from which each of you was born;
and the reed which I feel planted
on my head makes every importunate bird
flee from the gardens swift as the wind.
blocks.author: Horace

blocks.text: The ass may sometimes also be depicted with Priapus, because the ancients sacrificed it to him as a victim proper to him, either for the likeness of the great member between them, as Lactantius reports; or for the hatred that he bore this beast, because Silenus's ass with its importunate braying disturbed the pleasure that he was preparing to take from Vesta, whom he had found asleep at a certain feast of the Great Mother, as the fable related by Ovid tells; or else because, as is set down by those who write of the stars of Heaven, among which two in the sign of the Crab are called the Little Asses, an ass puffed up by the human speech given to it by Bacchus as a reward for having carried him over a certain river came to a contest with Priapus over the size of the natural member, and won, but to its very great harm, because Priapus, angered at this, killed it; and perhaps the ancients afterwards imitated this by sacrificing the ass to him.
Goat as a sign of Priapus

In Egypt, when they wished to show this god in their sacred signs, they depicted a billy goat, because it is read of this animal that, when only seven days old, it begins to mount, and is almost always ready for coupling; so it is no wonder that the member serving generation, worshipped by the ancients under the name of Priapus, was shown by it.
Apollodorus
Goat given to Bacchus

With the same animal Bacchus too was sometimes shown, because it is found that he changed into it when with the other gods he fled from the hands of Typhon into Egypt. Apollodorus writes that Jupiter changed Bacchus, still a little child, into a kid in order to hide him from Juno, and sent him by Mercury to the nymphs to be nursed, and therefore the goat was afterwards always a very welcome victim to Bacchus; or perhaps it was because this beast is greatly harmful to vines.
Gregory of Nazianzus

Besides, it is read that there was sometimes put in the hand of Bacchus a sceptre with the virile member on top, which perhaps showed the common power that Priapus had with him, although some give for it a certain other reason, so little decent that it does not seem to me that I ought to tell it, even if the interpreter of the first oration of Gregory of Nazianzus against Julian the Apostate reports it, and Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, hints at it too.

But I will rather say that the form of the member spoken of so many times appeared in the house of Tarquinius Priscus on the hearth, as the histories recount, and from it a maidservant of his wife, called Ocrisia, who had been seated there, rose pregnant with a son whom she bore in her time, and he was brought up with great care, as though he had been conceived of the seed of the Lar, the household god, and for that reason was to be a great man, as indeed he was, for he was the king of the Romans called Servius Tullius.
Lar
Lampridius
Tibullus

The Lar, or Lares, because there were many, were certain gods, or rather daemons, worshipped by the ancients in their own houses as guardians of them, in a certain place appointed for this besides the hearth, a place which, as I said already, was therefore called a Lararium. There were also other images there, as is read in Lampridius, that Alexander, emperor of Rome, had two Lararia. In the one, which was the larger, he kept Apollonius, Abraham and Orpheus, and had in the other, which was the smaller, Cicero and Virgil. Nor were the Lares guardians of private houses only but of the whole city also, and of the fields too outside, at the country estate, as Tibullus shows when he says:

lines: And you, Lares, once guardians of the rich,
now of the poor fields, accept the gifts
that humbly I offer and consecrate to you.
blocks.author: Tibullus

blocks.text: Figures offered to the Lares
Lares

Hence they were often worshipped at the crossroads of the streets, where on certain days they hung up for them some balls and little figures of wool; the former were for the servants, the latter for the others; and each person put up as many of the one and of the other as there were people in the house, so that when the Lares came they would catch hold of these, and not afterwards do harm to the persons; for some believed that they were daemons of the underworld, who, coming above ground when certain days were celebrated for them, would have done harm to the persons, had they not found something to amuse themselves with around the little figures I mentioned.

Or the ancients did this because others said that the Lares were our souls, already gone out of mortal bodies, who came to these feasts, and needed to find some body in which to rest; both of which are gathered from Festus.
Dog with the Lares

But for the most part the Lares were thought to be certain private daemons, guardians of houses, and were therefore depicted in the form of youths clothed in the skin of a dog, with the dog also at their feet; the ancients wishing to show by this animal that they were faithful and diligent guardians of houses, formidable to strangers and agreeable to those of the house, just as dogs are, according to Plutarch's report; and Ovid had already written the same, giving the reason why the dog is with the Lares. They were also sometimes clothed in tucked-up garments, turned over the left shoulder so that they come under the right, in order to be more nimble in their office, which was, as the same Plutarch says, to go seeking out all that each one did, and to spy diligently on all human deeds, so that through them the impious and wicked men might then be punished for their misdeeds.
Penates
Cicero

Like these Lares were the Penates, at least in guarding cities and keeping good watch over them; and some held that among the Romans they were Jupiter, Juno and Minerva. Others said that they were Apollo and Neptune, who built the walls of Troy. Cicero wrote that the Penates were certain numina in private houses, worshipped in the most secret parts of them. Hence Demipho in Terence says that he wishes to go home to greet the Penates, to return afterwards to the square to his business; and from this it is seen that these too, no less than the Lares, dwelt familiarly in houses; and their image, as Timaeus the historian writes, was two long, twisted rods of iron, like those that soothsayers held in their hands when they took auguries, with a certain earthen vessel; and the ancients kept these things among their sacred mysteries.
Dionysius

We read in Dionysius that in a certain small temple, not far from the Roman Forum, there were two figures of youths seated, each of whom held in his hand a pilum, which was a kind of spear once used by the Romans in war, with letters that said, Gods Penates, and that in many other ancient temples similar images of youths were seen in military dress and adornment; and such are to be seen also on some ancient medals.

Images of the gods Lares, that is, guardians of private houses and of individual cities, and observers of human deeds, or harmful gods; and image of the gods Penates, and their hieroglyph, signifying that they too are household gods and guardians of the cities and houses of private persons.
Genius
Horace

Besides these the Genius also was a household numen, proper to each man, whom some held to be the god of hospitality, of pleasure, of good times and of nature; and therefore it is said of one who gives himself a good time and does all that nature puts before him that he agrees with his Genius, but that he who does the contrary wrongs it. Horace, writing to Julius Florus, discourses on the instability of the things of the world and the various wills of men; then he poses a question, how it comes that of two brothers one will delight to be always at his ease, the other always to toil, and he answers thus:

lines: The Genius knows it, god of Nature,
who tempers and governs the natal star
of each and always accompanies him,
and changes often, so that he shows himself
now white and beautiful, now ugly and black.
blocks.author: Horace

blocks.text: Images of the good and the evil Genius, guardian and observer of the birth of man, of actions, of cities and of private places.
Censorinus
Double Genius

Others, such as Censorinus, have said that the Genius was worshipped by the ancients as the god of generation, either because he has the care of this, or because he was begotten together with us, and then always stays with us as our guardian; and they therefore held that there were as many Genii as there were men, as if one were given to each; or even that there were twice as many, and that each had two, one good and one bad: the former always exhorts and encourages to good, the latter to evil, just as we Christians say precisely of our guardian Angels and of the daemons, zealous tempters; except that these are not born with us, as the ancients understood that the Genii were born, each with each.
Genius of the Prince

The same they said also of the Lares, so that these differed little from one another; and therefore the Romans placed at the crossroads of the streets and in the country estates the Genius of Augustus with the Lares, and worshipped them together. Yet each one worshipped his own Genius by himself too, celebrating his birthday gladly and with much pleasure, but that of the Prince was revered by everyone more than all the others. Hence whoever had sworn falsely by the Genius of the Prince would have been punished at once, because among the ancients this was a most grave oath. And therefore Caligula, a very cruel prince, when putting many to death for the slightest causes, as Suetonius recounts, used to say this of some of those whom he had put to death, that he did so because they had never sworn by his Genius, as though they thereby despised him and showed that they judged him not worthy to be worshipped.
Iamblichus
Genius of places

The Genius was therefore a certain numen that from their very birth always accompanied men; and such numina were sometimes given to places also, as the philosopher Iamblichus says, showing that to those gods who are particular guardians and wardens of some place sacrifice must be made of those things that grow there, because the things governed are dearer than others to him who governs them.
Virgil
And Virgil describes a great serpent appearing to Aeneas while he is renewing the funeral rites for his father Anchises:

lines: whose back is green, painted
with golden spots, and the scaly
back, shining, resembles the heavenly bow,
which among the clouds, set against the Sun,
shows with great beauty many different colours.
blocks.author: Virgil

blocks.text: He leaves in doubt whether that was the genius of the place, or something else. Hence some have depicted the Genius in the form of a serpent, some others of a child, others of a youth, and others of an old man, as Cebes in his *Tablet*.
Sosipolis

Pausanias writes that the Eleans worshipped a certain god under the name of Sosipolis, which means Saviour of the City, as their Genius, proper to the country. He was in the temple of Lucina, and they sacrificed to him every year with certain ceremonies; and the reason for it was that the Arcadians having once marched against the Eleans on account of a certain war that was between them, a woman who had a little baby at the breast in her arms said to the captains of the Eleans: Sirs, this is my son, and when I bore him, not long ago, I was commanded in a dream to give him to you as a companion in war, and therefore here he is, I give him to you.

The Eleans did not at all disdain the good woman, but rather, taking it that this was not without some great mystery, took the baby and set him quite naked at the front of their army; where the Arcadians, who attacked them soon afterwards, saw him change at once into a great serpent, at which they were all so terrified that they dared go no further, but turning their backs took to flight, so that it was easy for the Eleans to drive them from their borders. Victorious for this reason, the Eleans called that child Sosipolis, crediting him with the preservation of the city. Serpent as he was, he seemed to thrust himself underground into a certain cavern, where the Eleans afterwards built a temple in the name of Lucina, and made also, as we would say, a chapel to Sosipolis, ordaining there honours and ceremonies proper to the one and to the other, because they believed that she had caused him to be born and had sent him for their safety.

His image, although he changed into a serpent, as I have said, was that of a child with a robe of various colours about him, loaded with stars, who held out with his hand the horn of plenty, because such he once appeared, as Pausanias says, to a man who afterwards reported it.
Medals of Hadrian

On some ancient medals of Hadrian, and of other emperors too, the Genius is seen depicted in the guise of a man, who holds out with his right hand a drinking vessel, which he appears to pour over an altar all adorned with flowers, and a whip hangs from his left side. And on other medals, also of Hadrian, is the image of a man of war with a robe wrapped around him down to mid-leg, who holds in his right hand something like a cup, as one who sacrifices, and has the horn of plenty in his left, and there are letters round about that say: To the Genius of the Roman People, which was perhaps to show that numen kept so secret by the Romans that they did not at all wish its name to be known, as I have said at another time.
Plane tree given to the Genius. Tibullus.

The ancients also made wreaths for the Genius from the branches of the plane tree, whose leaves are little unlike those of the vine; and sometimes also of various flowers, as is read in Tibullus, where he writes thus:

lines: Now with fair flowers girding his sacred locks
let the Genius come to see what in his honour
we do, celebrating his joyful name.
blocks.author: Tibullus

blocks.text: Euclid the Socratic

But since I have already said that the Genii were two, as Euclid the Socratic holds, according to Censorinus, let us now see the other, that is the evil one, how he was represented, for the good one is he whom we have drawn up to now. Of the evil one I have not found that the ancients made any statue or image; but it is indeed read that he appeared to many, and I shall portray him as they saw him, according to the example that the histories have preserved for us.
Plutarch. Appian. Florus.

Plutarch, Appian, Florus and others write that Brutus, having withdrawn at night into his room all alone, but with a lamp, to think by himself, as he was accustomed to do, saw an image of a man appear before him, all black and frightful, who said to him, when he asked, that he was his evil Genius, and soon vanished.
Evil Genius. Valerius Maximus.

Valerius Maximus writes that the wicked Genius appeared likewise to a certain Cassius, who was of the faction of Mark Antony, a few days before Caesar had him beheaded, and it was in the form of a very large man, of a dusky colour, with long hair and a horrid, unkempt, tousled beard.

And among the people of Temesa, once a people of Italy, in the Abruzzo, there was a very wicked and gloomy Genius, who was of a dusky and dark colour, wholly formidable to see, clothed in a wolf's skin, and who did such harm to those people that, as Pausanias recounts, and Suda also reports, they would have abandoned the country if the oracle had not shown them the way to appease the ghost of a companion of Ulysses, who was killed there because, being drunk, he had done violence to a young girl: for this was the wicked Genius who went about taking vengeance, of which Ulysses, passing by, took no account.
Evil Genius driven out

The people of Temesa therefore, by the counsel of the oracle, built a temple to him, and vowed to sacrifice to him every year one of the most beautiful girls of the city. As they did so, that diabolical Genius troubled them no more; but he stayed in the temple to receive the cruel sacrifice, until he was driven out of it by Euthymus, a man of great valour, who, arriving there just at the time when the wretched sacrifice was to be made, and having learned the cause of it, was moved to pity for the misery of that people, but more for the beautiful girl destined for the cruel sacrifice, for whom he felt himself at once kindled with a most ardent love, and therefore stopped everything. At this the cruel beast, enraged, came against him with the greatest fury, but Euthymus withstood it so well that after fighting a good while together he remained the victor, and chased it until he drove it to go and drown itself in the sea, and delivered that people from so great a calamity. For this reason the people gave him the girl he had freed for his wife, since he would have no other reward, and with the greatest feasting and gladness had the joyful wedding celebrated.

lines: This is she who is so much crucified
by the very ones who ought to give her praise,
blaming her unjustly and speaking ill of her.
blocks.author: Dante

blocks.text: Dante
Petrarch

So Dante speaks of Fortune, and it is from this that I wanted to begin, since I must now set out her image; for mortals blame her for everything that happens beyond their expectation, often taking badly what they ought rather to judge a great good. And it seems that they hold that the gaining and the loss of honours and riches come from Fortune, as does the overturning of all worldly things. Hence in Petrarch's canzone "Tacer non posso, e temo, &c." she speaks thus to him of herself:

lines: I have a different power from what you believe,
and I know how to make people glad and sad in a moment;
I am lighter than the wind:
and I rule and turn all those you see in the world.
blocks.author: Petrarch

blocks.text: Why Fortune is blamed
Fortune does not exist: Juvenal

And from this arise the endless reproaches that she hears of herself all day long; for it seems that these things, which we call the goods of fortune, go for the most part to him who deserves them least, and that he who would deserve them most remains miserably deprived of them. Whether this is good or bad I leave to be considered by whoever can see how many irksome cares, how many toils and how many dangers the goods of this world bring with them; for there are few who give thought to this, but almost all of us always seek to have them; and because we cannot satisfy our disordered desire, we then complain of Fortune, who, in the opinion of many, does not exist; hence Juvenal spoke of her thus:

lines: Where prudence is, Fortune has no power
at all, and her numen is
altogether empty; but we fools and madmen
still want to make her a goddess who dwells in Heaven.
blocks.author: Juvenal

blocks.text: Lactantius
Marcus Tullius

And Lactantius likewise says that Fortune is nothing but an empty name, which shows the little knowledge of men, agreeing with Marcus Tullius, who had written before him that the name of Fortune was introduced to cover human ignorance, which blames her for everything for which it cannot give an account.
But the ancients were no less mistaken about her than about the other gods, and so they worshipped her as a goddess who dispensed all worldly goods; and they thought that evil too came from her.
Two Fortunes
Pindar

For this reason two Fortunes were believed to exist, one good, the other bad; from the first came goods and felicities, and from the second all misfortunes and the other evils. Hence some have at times depicted Fortune with two faces: one was white, which showed the good one, the other black, which signified the bad one. And at Praeneste, where she had a temple much celebrated for the sure responses that were carried away from there, she was worshipped, according to Alexander ab Alexandro, under the image of two sisters. And for the same reason, perhaps, in Pindar too, as Plutarch reports, she turns two rudders with her hand.

Nevertheless it is for the most part held that there is only one Fortune, and her I shall depict according to the various designs left to us by the writers, beginning with the one Pausanias gives, where he writes that among the memorials of the ancients no statue of Fortune is found older than the one that Bupalus, an architect and excellent sculptor, made for the people of Smyrna, a people of Greece, in the form of a woman who had a polos on her head and held a cornucopia in one of her hands.

This statue showed what the office of Fortune is, which is to give and to take away riches, represented by the horn of plenty; and these things turn continually, as Heaven turns around the two poles. All those who have depicted Fortune, and made statues of her in whatever manner, have always shown the same thing afterwards, wishing to give us to understand that she has the government of the things down here, and that she can dispense them as she wishes.
Government of human affairs

This is read in Lactantius too, who describes how the ancients portrayed Fortune with the cornucopia and set a ship's rudder beside her, as though it belonged to her to give riches and the government of human affairs and temporal goods were in her hand, because in these there is no firmness, nor do they seem reasonably shared out, since the good for the most part suffer great hardships in them, and wicked men abound in them copiously.

Image of Fortune, giver and dispenser and patroness of riches and human goods, and governess of the things down here, in which there is no more firmness or stability than a ship tossed on the unstable waves of the sea can be said to have.
blocks.pt: Фортуна с рогом изобилия и рулём

blocks.text: Virgil
And so Fortune was said to be inconstant, blind, mad, and a much greater friend to the wicked than to the good, as is read in certain verses believed to be Virgil's, which in the vernacular run:

lines: O mighty Fortune, how often
you change, and how much power, alas, cruel one,
you usurp! You drive the good away from you
and call the wicked, yet you do not always
remain faithful even to these; you bring it about that more of your gifts
are granted to him who deserves them least,
depriving him who is worthy of them, and you so dispose
your affairs that sad poverty
oppresses the just with heavy hardships
and the wicked enjoy
all your goods. In their green age
you give men bitter death, and those
whom, burdened with years, life now wearies
(because you apportion the times with a will
not just), you still want to keep here.
To the impious goes what, through you, departs
from the better, and not in order to stay
with them: so you change in a little hour,
fragile, uncertain, faithless, and fleeting,
you through whom a man does not always rise or lie down.
blocks.author: Virgil

blocks.text: Martianus Capella

For these reasons the Thebans placed Plutus, as I said in his image, in the hands of Fortune, as though that god, who was believed to have all riches in his power, gave them and took them back again as it pleased her, whom Martianus Capella describes in the *Marriage of Philologia* in this way. There was, he says, a young girl, much more talkative than all the others, who never seemed to know how to stand still, all light and slender, and the wind, blowing from behind her, always made her swollen dress flutter in front.

Her name was Lot, according to some, and some called her Fortune, and some others Nemesis; and in her ample, wide lap she carried all the ornaments of the world, which she held out to some with a very swift hand, while from some, as if she were playing like a child, she used to pluck the hair, and some others she harshly struck on the head with a rod. And those same ones to whom she had at first shown herself so agreeable and friendly she afterwards struck on the head with her hand, as though she mocked them.
Horace

And Fortune is believed to do exactly this to us when she takes back her goods, leaving us disconsolate; and this would not happen if we did not make much greater account of what is hers than of what is our own: for riches belong to Fortune, and the virtues to us, and we always put the latter behind the former, as Horace says when he cries out indignantly thus:

lines: O citizens, foolish citizens,
seek riches first,
and leave the virtues behind them.
blocks.author: Horace

blocks.text: Good and bad Fortune

Then the ancients showed the good and joyful Fortune, which is when she offers us her goods, and the sad and disconsolate one, as we are when we are deprived of them, both together in this way, although the inscription speaks only of good Fortune, as is often seen on the ancient marbles of the Greeks. A woman sits, modestly dressed in the habit of a matron, sad in appearance and disconsolate; in front of her stands a beautiful young woman, comely to look at, who gives her her right hand, and behind is a girl, who stands with one hand resting on the seat [?] of the matron. The matron shows past Fortune, and therefore is sad; the young woman who gives her her hand and shows herself joyful is present Fortune, and the girl behind, resting on the seat, is the one who is coming, or is to come.
qm: The print reads "fede" ("appoggiata alla fede della matrona", scan 0419, and again below); this is evidently a misprint for "sede" (seat), and the translation follows that reading.

blocks.text: Images of joyful and sad Fortune, or of Fortune past, present, and to come, judged by the ancients, although she is only an imagined name, to be greater than all their false gods and the patroness of the things down here; and this numen the ancients imagined as an excuse for their imprudences.
Nemesis

But before I go on speaking further of Fortune, I want to say who Nemesis was; for these two are very like each other, so much so that some have believed them to be one and the same thing, as can be seen from what I have just reported of Martianus Capella. Nevertheless each was worshipped separately, and the one and the other had images different from each other, as will appear from my design.
Ammianus Marcellinus
Nemesis, then, was a goddess who was believed to show each person what was right for him to do; and Ammianus Marcellinus speaks of her thus:

lines: This is the goddess who punishes the wicked and rewards the good, knowing all things, so that the ancient theologians imagined her the daughter of Justice, who from a certain secret part of Eternity stays looking upon the works of mortals.
blocks.author: Ammianus Marcellinus

blocks.text: Macrobius
Rhamnusia

Macrobius says of her that she was worshipped as the avenger of pride, and in his usual manner he brings her back to the power of the Sun. For the Sun is of such a nature that wherever it appears it dims the splendour of every other light, and often makes appear and shine what before stayed hidden and seemed dark. So Nemesis likewise oppresses the over-proud, raises the humble, and helps them to live well; and in sum this goddess was believed to punish all those who grew too proud of the good they had. The poets often called her Rhamnusia, from a certain place in the country of Athens, where she had a most beautiful marble idol.
Adrasteia

She was also called Adrasteia at times, from King Adrastus, because he was the first to set up a temple to her. The ancients depicted her with wings, because they believed that she was ready for everyone with marvellous speed, and beside her they put a ship's rudder, and a wheel under her feet.

Image of the goddess Nemesis, who points out good works and severely punishes the proud and the wicked; a courteous and generous giver, who rewards good deeds, being held to be the knower of all of them: daughter of Justice, who teaches us to use measure and good sense in our actions.

Nemesis was sometimes depicted as holding a bridle in one hand and in the other a piece of wood with which one measures, wishing thereby to show that men must put a bridle on the tongue and do everything with measure, as two Greek verses say, which were once made on this statue, and in the vernacular their sense is this:

lines: With this bridle and with this measure
I, Nemesis, show that everyone
must rein in the tongue, and never do
anything unless he has first measured it well.

blocks.text: Pausanias
Ausonius

Pausanias writes that Nemesis was a goddess exceedingly hostile to insolent and over-proud men, and he continues thus. The barbarians were once punished by her wrath: despising the Athenians, and having come into their lands as though they had already utterly defeated them, they had a most beautiful marble brought there in order to make a proud trophy of it afterwards; but it all turned out the opposite, for the Athenians remained the victors, and Phidias then made out of that marble, brought by the barbarians, an idol of the goddess Nemesis, on which Ausonius wrote an epigram, pretending that the goddess herself says that it was made as a sign of the victory of the Greeks, and to show that she did not leave the vain pride of the Persians unpunished.

This idol had on its head a crown carved with stags and small images of Victory, and held an ash branch in the left hand and in the right a vase with some Ethiopians carved inside it; of which things Pausanias says that he cannot give any account, nor even know what to think of them, and I know even less.
Nemesis without wings
Catullus

The same Pausanias adds that the statues of Nemesis did not have wings at first, as they afterwards had among the people of Smyrna, who were the first to make her winged, in the likeness of Cupid, because they believed that she had a great deal to do with lovers, as though she punished those of them who were too haughty and proud of their beauty, as Ovid shows in the fable of Narcissus. And Catullus likewise, after begging Licinius, a very beautiful youth, at length to come to him, says at the end: take care not to hold my prayers in little account and despise me, lest Nemesis, the terrible goddess, should some time punish you for it afterwards.
Justice
A. Gellius
Justice sees everything

Because, then, this goddess punished mortals for their proud and unjust deeds, some believed her to be the same as Justice. Her image is described by Chrysippus, according to Aulus Gellius, in the form of a beautiful virgin, terrible in aspect, neither proud nor humble, but such that with honest severity she shows herself worthy of all reverence, with eyes of most acute sight; hence Plato said that Justice sees everything, and that she was called by the ancient priests the avenger of all things.

Image of Justice, guardian of the good and punisher of the wicked; and image of Justice trampling on and chastising Injury; and a hieroglyph denoting this Justice, and what she must be, appear, and do.
Apuleius
What judges ought to be

And Apuleius swears by the eye of the Sun and of Justice together, as though the eye of Justice saw no less than that of the Sun. We are to understand that all this must be in the ministers of justice, because they must penetrate with most acute sight as far as the hidden and concealed truth, and be pure like chaste virgins, so that neither precious gifts nor false flatteries nor anything else can corrupt them, but with the firmest severity they must always judge by reason; and they must show themselves terrible and fearsome to the guilty and the wicked, and pleasant and kind to the good and innocent.

Some have also put a balance in the hand of Justice, and sometimes that bundle of bound rods with the axe which the lictors carried before the Roman consuls. And at times Justice was depicted by the ancients in this way as well. A virgin sat naked on a square stone, and held in one hand a balance and in the other a naked sword [?].
qm: The print has a comma, not a full stop, after "una spada nuda", and the next sentence ("Scriue Diodoro, ch'in certa parte dell'Egitto...") begins with a capital letter; the translation closes the sentence at "naked sword" and starts a new one with Diodorus.

blocks.text: Diodorus writes that in a certain part of Egypt, where the Gates of Truth were, there was also a statue of Justice, which had no head; and he gives no explanation of it, nor shall I, as I come to say that in Egypt they depicted Justice in this way as well. They painted her left hand stretched out and open, because this is naturally colder and lazier than the right, and therefore less able to do injury to anyone.

Hence, among the other things carved on the chest of Cypselus, Pausanias writes, there was a beautiful woman who dragged another behind her, an ugly one, holding her tight by the neck with her left hand and with the right striking her harshly with a stick; and that the first was Justice and the second Injury. For just judges must always keep Injury oppressed, so that no wrong is ever done to anyone; they must see to it that the truth is never hidden from them, and so hear everything that each person says in his own defence, and not condemn the accused on the words of the accusers alone, if they do not wish to be like that judge whom Apelles once painted, as Lucian relates, after he had been freed by Ptolemy, king of Egypt. Ptolemy had been about to put him to death, having believed Antiphilus too foolishly, who out of envy had accused Apelles of being privy to a certain rebellion; but the truth was afterwards discovered by one of the conspirators, and the king, having learned of the deception, freed Apelles and gave him a hundred talents, and willed that Antiphilus, who had accused him wrongly, should afterwards be Apelles' slave forever.
Painting by Apelles
Calumny
Repentance

Apelles, then, wishing to show the danger he had been in, painted a most beautiful panel, which was afterwards called the Calumny of Apelles, in this way. One sat in the manner of a judge, who had long ears like those of an ass, as it is read that King Midas had them. Beside him two women, one on each side, seemed to be saying I know not what very softly in his ears; one of them was Ignorance, the other Suspicion. And he held out his hand to Calumny, who came toward him in the form of a beautiful, adorned woman, but who showed in her aspect that she was full of anger and disdain; in her left hand she had a lit torch, and with her right she dragged behind her by the hair a naked youth, who lamented miserably, raising his clasped hands to Heaven. Before her went Malice (*Liuore*), that is, Envy, who was an old man, thin and pale, like one who has been long ill; and behind her came two women who seemed to flatter her, making much of her beauty and adorning her all the while as much as they could; one was called Fraud, and the name of the other was Treachery. Behind these followed another woman called Repentance, with a few rags about her, all worn and torn, who, weeping abundantly, afflicted herself beyond measure and seemed to want to die of shame, because she saw Truth coming.

Panel of Calumny painted by Apelles, in which there is the judge with the ears of an ass, denoting Ignorance, and two women speak into his ears, one of whom is Ignorance, the other Suspicion. The old man who goes before Calumny is the envious man, and the one whom Calumny holds by the hair is the Calumniated. Of the two women who accompany Calumny, one is Fraud and the other Treachery. Of the two women below, one is Repentance, looking at Truth, the effect of calumniating, which as its recompense awaits shame, harm, and disgrace.
Envy
Silius Italicus
Horace

Thus Lucian describes the Calumny once painted by Apelles, and he gathers from it that this is nothing other than a false accusation, believed by the judge, against someone who is not present to state his case; which for the most part is caused by Envy, and therefore Apelles put Envy before her. And Envy is the worst sickness there can be of the human mind, because it not only does harm to others, but also does great harm to the envious themselves. Hence Silius Italicus puts among the plagues and monsters that are in hell envy, which squeezes its throat with both hands; and therefore Horace did well to say that

lines: The tyrants of Sicily did not know how
to find a greater torment than Envy.
blocks.author: Horace

blocks.text: Virgil
For, as some verses believed to be Virgil's say, rendered into the vernacular in this way:

lines: Envy is a poison that devours
the marrow and sucks out all the blood.
So the envious man has his due punishment;
for while another's fortune grieves him,
he sighs, trembles, and roars like a lion,
showing that his wretched soul is full
of cruel hatred, which leads him
to look on another's good with a crooked eye.
So inside he turns to ice, and outside
he is bathed in fury,
which can make others aware of his pain;
and, armed with a tongue of venom,
he always bites and blames whatever he gazes at.
A pale colour tinges his face,
which gives a sure sign of inner grief,
and the wretched body becomes such
that it seems to be destroyed and undone.
Whatever he sees brings him hatred and disdain:
so he flees the light, and everything turns
to ill for him, and with equal
displeasure he shuns food, drink wearies him,
he never sleeps, he never has rest,
and his heart is always gnawed
by that envious rage, which
can never have an end; and against its grave sickness
no physician's remedy avails.
blocks.author: Virgil

blocks.text: Images of Envy, who harms herself, since the envious man wastes away seeing another's prosperity, and stops his ears against another's praises, and squeezes his throat to choke himself, seeing them exalted; and this is the worst of vices.
Ovid
And Ovid, depicting her in the form of a woman (for, as we said a little earlier in speaking of the painting of Apelles, the Greeks depicted her as a man), describes her thus:

lines: Pale is her face, her body thin and dry,
her eyes squint, and her tooth is rusty,
her breast burns with bitter gall, and foul
venom fills her tongue, and she never feels
any pleasure except in another's grief:
then Envy laughs, who otherwise
shows herself every hour pained and sad,
and always vigilant and wakeful for another's harm.
blocks.author: Ovid

blocks.text: And in describing her house first, gloomy, cold, and murky, he had said that she stayed there eating snakes. Plutarch wrote at some length on envy, and the great Basil, in a speech on it, says that the envious are like vultures and flies. For as those, flying, pass over joyful fields and flowery meadows and do not alight except where they see some stinking body, and in this too, leaving the whole parts, go seeking the corrupt and spoiled ones, so the envious never look at what in others deserves to be praised, or pretend not to see it, and give their attention only to what can be blamed in some way.
Momus
Aesop

So Momus was believed to act among the gods; he too was a god among the ancients, and was born, according to Hesiod, of Sleep and Night: he never did anything himself, but looked at what the other gods did, and freely reproved and blamed whatever was not done to his taste. Hence Aesop wrote, and Aristotle reports it, that Momus blamed the maker of the bull, saying that he was ill advised to put its horns on its head, for he should have put them on its shoulders, so that it could strike with greater force.

Image of Momus, god of reproof, or slander, and of blame, son of Sleep and Night, signifying that detractors are good for nothing and never do anything, but only blame the works of others, never looking at anything but what is open to reproof, and never at what is praiseworthy, like moles, which look neither at the sun nor at the day, but only at darkness and gloom.

And of man he said, as Lucian relates, that whoever made him greatly erred in not making a little window in his breast, so that one could easily see what he had in his heart. In Venus he found nothing to find fault with, as Philostratus writes, except that her slippers made too much noise when she walked. His image is described by certain Greek epigrams in the form of an old man, thin and dry, quite pale, with open mouth, and bent toward the earth, which he keeps striking with a stick that he has in his hand, perhaps because all the gods of the ancients were called sons of the earth.
Euripides
Aelian

Among these gods, Momus, god of reproof and blame, performed the office that some among us perform, who are therefore likewise called Momuses: moved only by a desire to speak ill of others at their pleasure, and without any reason, they blame whatever they see. This comes for the most part, as I have already said, from Envy, which, as Euripides said and Aelian reports, is an exceedingly wretched, wicked, and shameful thing; and it is read that the ancients designated it by depicting an eel, because this, as the same Aelian says, keeps by itself and never goes with the other fish.
Fraud
Dante

As for Fraud, whom Apelles depicted in the form of a woman, Dante drew her with the face only of an upright and just man, but with the rest of the body all that of a serpent, spotted with various colours, and ending in the tail of a scorpion. His words are these:

lines: And that filthy image of fraud
came on, and landed its head and chest,
but did not draw its tail onto the bank.
Its face was the face of a just man,
so benign was its skin on the outside,
and a serpent's were both parts of the trunk.
It had two paws, hairy up to the armpits,
the back, the chest, and both flanks
it had painted with knots and little wheels.
With more colours, underlaid and overlaid,
there never were Tartar or Turkish cloths,
nor were such webs laid on the loom by Arachne.
blocks.author: Dante

blocks.text: Nature of the fraudulent
Pine for Fraud

The explanation of this image is that the nature of deceiving and fraudulent men is to show themselves benign, pleasant, and modest in appearance and in words, but to be otherwise in deeds, so that all their works in the end show themselves full of deadly poison. For this reason the ancients at times also put the pine, wishing to depict Fraud: for this tree is tall and straight, and always green, and beautiful and pleasing to see, but then often harmful to whoever rests in its shade or passes under it without other regard, because its fruits, already ripe and therefore very hard, fall from the high branches and, if they chance to strike him on the head, hit him so fiercely that they kill him or at least make him feel very grave pain, if they happen instead to wound him in some other part of the body.

Image of Fraud according to Dante, which denotes that the fraudulent and deceivers, under the cloak and face of the pleasant, modest, and loving, seek to arrive at their evil designs, being inwardly poisoned with every vice, fraud, and deceit.

But let us return to the image of Fortune, from which Nemesis led me astray; and I, passing then from one thing to another, did not remember to return to her before now, when nothing more remains for me to say about the painting of Apelles. Apelles, painting Fortune too, placed her seated, and being asked why he had done so, answered that he had never seen her standing; and among the Latins to stand (*stare*) means not only to be firm but also to be on one's feet, and from this he made a witticism, because Fortune is called changeable and unstable.
Horace

Wishing to show this in her image, the ancients, as Eusebius writes, depicted her sitting on a large ball and added wings to her, which carry her most swiftly now to one person, now to another. Hence Horace sings thus of her, his verses drawn into our language:

lines: Unstable Fortune
attends to a cruel game,
and always plays to the harm of mortals,
without any rule
she changes things, and renders
honour to this one, to that one gives grave ills,
and then those who
were by her favour
first glad and content
she makes wretched and discontent,
and, changing almost every hour,
to one she gives, from another takes away,
whether her wishes be kind or adverse to them.
So I thank her
when she stays still for me,
and gladly enjoy her goods.
But not so much that I do not remember
my own, and that my thoughts too
have no firm hope in them.
So then, if she flies away,
spreading her light wings,
whatever she ever gave me
I refuse, and my mind returns, secure,
to that sole virtue
which contents it,
and does not try to have greater riches.
blocks.author: Horace

blocks.text: Cebes
Artemidorus

Cebes, in that tablet in which he painted all human life, depicts Fortune as a blind and mad woman, who stands with her feet on a round stone. And Artemidorus has at times placed her seated on a column lying on its side, and sometimes depicts her beautiful and adorned, and sometimes dirty and badly dressed, and with her hand on a ship's rudder. And in this way we often see her on ancient medals and on ancient marbles.
Galen
Galen likewise, when he exhorts the young to the study of letters, says this of her:

lines: Wishing to set the wickedness of Fortune before our eyes in paintings and statues, the ancients were not content to depict her in the form of a woman (though this ought well to have been enough to show that she was mad and wicked and never stayed in one purpose); they added a round ball under her feet, depicting her without eyes, and then gave her a rudder in her hand, as though blindly and without any foresight she governed the things of the world.
blocks.author: Galen

blocks.text: Pacuvius
Some verses of Pacuvius, which are read in the books of Cicero's *Rhetoric* and run thus in the vernacular, also draw Fortune very well and likewise explain her image:

lines: Mad, blind, and beastly is Fortune,
according to what the philosophers have said,
who have set her upon a stone that turns and rolls;
so wherever this
leans, she goes swiftly, and knows not where
nor sees; hence with reason she was called blind.
And because she changes too often
they have called her mad, and beastly
she has been called because she does not know
who is worthy and who not, who good and who bad.
blocks.author: Pacuvius

blocks.text: Good Fortune

Besides this, the caduceus was sometimes depicted with a cap on top, which had two small wings, one on each side, and with two cornucopias that embraced the caduceus itself; and this painting signified, according to some, that good Fortune goes almost always together with Eloquence and Learning. In sum, she was believed to be of such strength that there was no lack of those who said that virtue is worth little without her; and that although virtue leads to high undertakings and a glorious name, we shall never arrive there, or only with difficulty, if she does not accompany us, supposing, as the ancients believed, that Fortune is some numen, which in worldly things can do a great deal.
Seneca

And that we ourselves are to ourselves good fortune or bad, according as we know well or badly how to govern ourselves and to seize the good that is presented to us or let it go. Hence Seneca writes to his Lucilius that those are mistaken who judge that any good or evil comes to us from Fortune; for although she gives the material of the one and the other, and some beginnings to things that may afterwards turn out well or ill, nevertheless our mind can do much more than she, and draws its affairs as it wishes, so that it is itself to itself the cause of either a happy or a wretched life.
Ausonius
Occasion

And so, when we seize on what is bad, we ought to complain of our own incapacity and our poor sight over all the misfortunes that befall us afterwards, not of Fortune: as the ancients also showed in the image of Occasion, whom some make one and the same with Fortune; but if these two are not one and the same thing, they are very like each other, as can be seen from the portrait of this one, who was made a goddess by the ancients, perhaps so that, from her image, revered and often looked at, everyone should learn to take things in time, because these change with time and go away, leaving him who did not know how to take them full of sadness and repentance.

The image of Occasion was as follows: a naked woman stood with her feet on a wheel, or on a round ball, and had her long hair all turned over her forehead, so that the nape was left uncovered and as if bald, and at her feet she had wings, as Mercury is painted, and with her was another woman, all grieving, sad in aspect, and full of repentance. Such an idol was once made by Phidias, and an epigram of Ausonius on it is read, in which he describes Occasion as I have said, and gives her Repentance as a companion. For whoever lets the good occasion pass that presents itself in any matter has afterwards nothing but to repent and complain of himself.
The god Kairos
Posidippus
Ausonius

She whom the Latins called Occasion and Opportunity, and revered as a goddess, was called by the Greeks Opportune Time, and so was made by them a god, not a goddess, and his name was Kairos, since this word among the Greeks means opportunity of time, as Pausanias also writes, where he says that an altar was consecrated to him among the Eleans, and that a certain ancient poet in a hymn made for him calls him the youngest of all the sons of Saturn. So the god Kairos of the Greeks was the same as the Occasion of the Latins; of him Posidippus made an epigram describing his image, from which Ausonius perhaps took the subject of his own when he depicted Occasion, for they are wholly alike, except that Posidippus puts a razor in the hand of his god, and Ausonius gives his goddess Repentance besides as a companion. Callistratus too, a noble sculptor, made the god Kairos in the form of a youth in his most flourishing age, beautiful and comely, with his locks scattered in the wind, and in all the rest exactly as Posidippus describes him.

One must, then, keep one's eyes open and one's hands ready to lay hold of things when Occasion shows them to us, because she soon turns, and turns the bald nape to whoever did not know how to thrust his hands into the long locks she has over her forehead, and goes away on the swiftest feet.

Hieroglyph denoting that good Fortune almost always goes with Eloquence and with Learning, and the image of Occasion, and opportunity, called by the Greeks the god Kairos, whom whoever does not seize when he presents himself afterwards seeks in vain and repents.
Fortune of the Scythians

The Scythians showed almost the same in the image of their Fortune, for, as Quintus Curtius reports, they depicted her without feet, but put wings about her hands, because with these she gives and offers goods, but with such speed that scarcely has anyone stretched out his hand to take them than she has already flown away. Besides, although Fortune sometimes joins us hand in hand, she never lets us seize the feathers she has around her hands, because she wishes to be able to fly off again at her pleasure, and to fly off without much delay, since she does not know how to stop, and the felicities that come from her last little.

Image of Fortune among the Scythians, signifying her speed and instability in worldly things, and that one must go along with Occasion, because she flies away swiftly, and then is followed in vain, and in vain one repents of occasions lost and neglected.
Fortune of glass

Hence it was that some once made her of glass, as Alexander ab Alexandro writes; for as glass breaks at once at every slight obstacle, so the favours of Fortune quickly come to the ground. But the ancients did not for this cease to believe in her; on the contrary, they showed such trust in her that they always wanted to have her with them, above all the princes and the emperors; for these kept in their most secret chamber a gilded idol of Fortune, and worshipped it as a sacred thing, and also wanted it to be with them every time they went out in public.
Idol of Fortune with the emperors. Spartianus.

Hence Spartianus writes that the emperor Severus, having come to the extreme of life, wished to arrange that there should be two of these sacred statues of Fortune, so that each of his sons, who were two, should have one to accompany him and stay with him always; but being unable to attend to it, because his illness weighed on him too heavily, he commanded as he died that the sacred idol of Fortune should be placed in turn in the secret chamber of his sons, one day with the one and the next with the other, as though this were a sign of the empire divided equally between them.
The emperor Antoninus Pius

And the emperor Antoninus Pius, according to the same Spartianus, feeling himself near to death, commanded that the gilded statue of Fortune should be carried into the chamber of Marcus Antoninus, which was the surest sign of the empire transferred to him, as though the emperor who was dying, without saying anything else, designated him in this way as his successor.

Some, and very well, have painted Fortune upon a great tree with a long stick in her hand, with which she goes beating down its fruits, which are sceptres of kings, mitres, purses, ships, ploughs, and other things that denote dignities and all the human arts. Below one sees a great multitude of persons of every sort and rank, who wait to catch the fruit that comes down upon them. And one sees that someone of royal stock, if a plough touches him, must from the prince that he was become a poor farmer, whereas a peasant, if a sceptre or some purse falls upon him, becomes a prince and rich: so that one must settle oneself in a good place, so that, Fortune prospering, some good fortune may chance to touch us.
Pausanias

Pausanias writes that in Greece, among the Eleans, Fortune had a temple, in which there was a very large idol of her in wood, all gilded except the hands and feet, which were of marble. And he then tells also of some other statues of Fortune made by the Greeks in various places, but does not report them, because they have nothing notable beyond what has already been said.
Fortune helpful to Love

I shall rather tell of the one that was at Aegira, a city of Achaea, although I have already spoken of it in the image of Cupid. It was made in this way. On one side she had the cornucopia, and held it in her hand, on the other the god Cupid; and this signified, as Pausanias interprets it, that it avails lovers little to be beautiful, comely, and gentle when they do not have Fortune with them, which seems to mean that in Love one needs, no less than in other things, to have luck and good fortune; and alas, it does mean this.

But to this must be added also that Fortune must carry the cornucopia with her, because without it she will be of little help to Love, thanks to the avaricious female mind, which regards neither beauty, nor virtue, nor gentility, but bends only to precious gifts. Hence one can say with assurance that whoever has gold, silver, and precious gems, all gifts of Fortune and shown by the cornucopia, will always be fortunate and happy in love.

Image of Fortune at Aegira, signifying that in Love good fortune and riches are wanted, otherwise the desired wish is not obtained. But I believe that, in this as in all actions, one must have virtues, for these make good Fortune, because there is no Fortune at all, but it is an imagined name.
To women
Admonition
Against avaricious women

Forgive me, women, that zeal for your honour now forces me to speak with you in this way, far more than the harm which I have already felt several times from your avaricious desires. Are you not ashamed (and I speak only to those who do it) to give yourselves for a price no differently from the way beasts are sold? Although, like them, you remain in the free power of whoever buys you, you do come back again, so that you can give yourselves now to one and now to another, according to which offers the greater price; but your honour and your good name remain always a prey to infamy, to blame, and to shame.

And if perhaps you were to say to me: what does it matter more that we are shameless for a price than for love alone? In either case, for this as for that, we lose our honour, which you men have confined within the narrowest limits, so that if we are willing to stay within them there will be no love for us: and how then do you want us to set about doing your pleasures for love? I would answer you that there are some deeds which, though perhaps not very good in themselves, yet brought to their end by means of virtue, content him who does them, and are also for the most part praised; whereas he who acts viciously neither contents himself while he stays hidden, nor, when he is made known, finds anyone who praises him.

Love is a virtue, and Avarice is a vice. Therefore what you do for love not only does not trouble your mind, aware of having acted virtuously, but is praised besides by whoever knows of it. But what avaricious desire draws you to goads you always and never gives you rest, so that you always feel a certain remorse which says to you: ah, you did wrong after all. And when it is afterwards learned by others, from gentle and honoured women you become vile and infamous, and often the name of honest gentlewoman is changed to that of shameless harlot, which never happens to her who for love pleases him who loves her; for only those who do it for hire are called harlots.

The limits set to your honour are not at all as narrow as some of you perhaps think, that love is forbidden to you; on the contrary, it is given to you as your own, since by yourselves, without a man, you are worth little. And how will you approach a man with pleasure to both, if love does not come between to bind you together? Therefore Love is not taken from you: but do you know what is taken from you? To do injury to Love, as many do, bargaining over that which they should do for his sake alone.

So it is not for love, nor because, overcome by human frailty, they cannot resist carnal passions (things which very well cover and excuse our errors), that they throw themselves into the arms of the one they make a show of loving, but because they are too greedy and rapacious, and think that by giving themselves to many, in order to have from many, they can better fill their avaricious and insatiable desires. And therefore anyone who has something to give can easily enjoy them.

For this reason, then, Cupid is joined to Fortune, who holds the cornucopia, and this shows also the little firmness of such women, because avaricious women are no less changeable in love than Fortune is. To her image I return, and I leave you, women, who live in your shameful errors; and to those who are far from them I promise to say one day all the good in the world of them, and in such a way that perhaps they will even set some store by it.
Gregorio Giraldi

So, besides the designs of Fortune made up to here, I find that some have painted her at sea, where she sails among troubled waves; some have set her on the sharp top of a high rock or of a mountain, so that every little wind that blows makes her turn. And I believe that these were modern paintings, because I find no mention of them made by the ancients, as was likewise the case with this one, which Giraldi reports, writing on the gentiles, where he says thus:

lines: Some in our times, with a quite beautiful invention, have depicted Fortune on horseback, running away at great speed, and Fate, or Destiny, as it seems one should call it, follows her, holding, like an archer, the bow with the arrow to wound her. This painting shows the speed of Fortune, as though she never rested, but ran away always, driven off by Fate, because where Destiny is, Fortune has no place.
blocks.author: Giraldi

blocks.text: Image of Fortune on horseback running swiftly, followed by Fate and Destiny, denoting her speed, and that where these are, she has no power or firmness.
Apuleius
Apuleius makes her one and the same with Isis, when he pretends that to him, returned from an ass to a man, the priest of the goddess speaks thus:

lines: Now you are under the protection of Fortune, not of that one who is blind, but of the one who sees, and gives light to the other gods as well with her splendour.
blocks.author: Apuleius

blocks.text: Fortune as the Moon

And we can say that he therefore meant good Fortune; under her name Macrobius understood the Moon, shown through Isis, as has already been said in her image, because she can do much in the bodies down here, which are subject to the various chances of fortune and go on changing continually. Putting the Moon and Fortune together, then, as though they were one and the same goddess, from whom come the birth and death of things, we may say that Pausanias was not at all mistaken when he said that Pindar would easily make him believe that Fortune was one of the Parcae, and could do much more than her sisters. Though it seems to me that the Parcae agree much more with Fate, or Destiny, whichever we wish to call it, than with Fortune, because this is fixed and certain, just as they too are immutable, since in spinning the life of mortals they assign to each the determined time of dying.
Bonus Eventus

But what has this to do with images? Nothing. Let us leave it, then, and speak of Bonus Eventus, that is, prosperous outcome and happy end of undertakings, for the idol of him among the Romans stood on the Capitol with that of good Fortune, as Pliny writes, in the form of a cheerful and well-dressed young man, who held in his right hand a cup and in his left an ear of corn and a poppy.
Favour

And with Fortune goes Favour too, who was likewise worshipped by the ancients, because he seems to come for the most part from her, although he is born many times of beauty also, and often of virtue, and in sum of all those things that make us pleasing to others and win us favour, which often makes us grow proud. For the more things succeed happily for men, the more they raise themselves, and, soaring on the wings of human favour, climb above others until the wheel turns; then, falling headlong, they are despised no less than they were revered before.
Timid Favour

Therefore let everyone beware of trusting too much in this frail and light Favour, because he soon passes, as his image shows us, which was that of a youth with wings: either because by prosperous and joyful things he rises so high that he no longer deigns to look down, so that he was also painted blind, since men seem to look no more at anyone, or very little, once they are raised to great honours; or because he stays little with us, but soon passes away. And therefore he stood with his feet on a wheel, since he imitates Fortune; and as she turns, so he turns likewise, and goes always wherever she carries her goods, showing himself nevertheless timid, because he wants every hour to climb higher than is fitting for him, pushed by Flattery, who always accompanies him.
Behind him goes Envy as well, but with slow and sluggish steps; she always looks with a crooked eye on the Felicity of others, but Felicity is blessed, and does not fear her at all.
