And reading in the same author, and in Aelian too, about the nature of this animal, I find that the ancient sculptors gave women a fine and holy admonition by putting the tortoise under the foot of Venus; for the tortoise knows the danger she runs when she couples with the male, seeing that she must turn over with her belly upwards, and the male, when he has done his business, goes away and leaves her, who cannot right herself by herself, as prey to the other animals, but above all to the eagle.

For this reason she abstains from coition with the greatest continence and, fleeing the male, puts safety before libidinous pleasure, to which she is nevertheless forced to consent afterwards, touched by a certain herb that sets her wholly aflame with lust, so that after that she no longer fears anything. Women too, then, must consider to what danger they expose themselves when they lose their honour, and for this reason they must flee lascivious pleasures and libidinous appetites, unless the duty of marriage forces them to these for the succession of new offspring.

Images of Venus, of Cupid, of Jocus and of the goat, which signify generation; and the image of the tortoise, a hieroglyph, which denotes the danger of married women and of women in childbirth, and what their duty must be in the care of the family and in bringing up children, and that silence is necessary to women above every virtue.
Venus with Mercury
Peitho

Besides the Graces and the Cupids, Plutarch writes, the ancients were accustomed to place with the statue of Venus that of Mercury too, wishing in this way to give to understand that amorous unions have need of sweet and gentle attentions and of pleasant words, because these often give rise to Love between people and preserve it. For this reason they also placed among the Graces who went with Venus the one who was called Peitho by the Greeks and Suada by the Latins, and she was the goddess of persuasion.
Megarians
Ovid

Suada, in the temple of Jupiter among the Eleans in Greece, presented a crown to Venus, who was rising from the sea and was received by Cupid, as I said above. And the Megarians likewise placed the idol of Suada in the temple of Venus; and the first who had the one and the other worshipped among the Athenians was Theseus, as Pausanias relates, after he had gathered into one city those people who before were scattered through the fields. In other places of Greece too there were temples of the goddess Suada; from which it can be seen that she too was worshipped by the ancients and often placed in the company of Venus, because, as Ovid says:

lines: Venus was the first who made
men refined out of the rude beings that they were.
blocks.author: Ovid

blocks.text: Arcadians

The first eloquence was that of lovers, who sought to persuade the young women they loved to be easy to their desires, and, to please them too, found a thousand fine things that were not known before. So the Arcadians, worshipping Venus, called her Contriver and Inventor, and rightly, says Pausanias, seeing that on account of the pleasures that come from Venus men have found various ways of drawing beautiful young women to their wishes, afterwards leading a joyful life with them, because Venus seems to care only for cheerful and pleasant things. For this reason Jupiter in Homer warns her to keep away from sad wars, when she wished to help Aeneas against Diomedes, who wounded her in the hand, because these things are proper to Mars and to Minerva, not to her, to whom belongs the care of amorous pleasures.
Lactantius

But not for this did the ancients refrain from depicting Venus armed. The reason for this, as Lactantius writes, was that while the Lacedaemonians were besieging Messene, the Messenians went out secretly to sack Lacedaemon and to plunder all the country round about, believing that they could do it easily, since all the fighting men of the place had gone to the siege. But their plan did not succeed for them; for the Lacedaemonian women, who learned of this, armed themselves, all those who were fit for it, and going against the enemy not only defended the city and the country from being sacked but also put the Messenians to rout and forced them to go back.

In the meantime the Lacedaemonians, having noticed the deceit of the enemy, went out to meet them; but since the Messenians were returning, fleeing by another road, they could not find them, and so came upon their own women, all armed. The women, thinking them to be the enemy, were drawing up in order to fight, when they revealed themselves and made themselves seen by their men, who recognised them at once, and all went immediately to embrace one another. And because there was no time then for each man to find his own, they amorously took their pleasure together for a while, armed as they were, each with the one that chanced to fall at his feet, as though it were the dearest and most welcome reward that they could give to those valiant women warriors for their labours.
Ausonius

So, in memory of this event and of the fine deed done by the women, the Lacedaemonians set up a temple to Venus with a statue of her armed, on which Ausonius made a fine epigram, and he imagines that Pallas, seeing Venus armed, as she herself also always went, wishes to come again to a contest with her, even under the judgement of Paris; but Venus mocks her as rash, for having the audacity to challenge her now that she sees her armed, if she was defeated by her already when she was naked. The epigram, put into the vernacular, is this.

lines: Pallas, seeing at Sparta the fair
Venus armed in the manner of a warrior,
said: "Now it is time to end that
quarrel which makes you go so haughty,
and let Paris be the judge of it." And she
answered: "Ah, rash one, does your spirit
then hope to conquer me, armed, now,
when naked and unarmed I conquered you before?"
blocks.author: Ausonius

blocks.text: Image of Venus armed, of Venus Victorious and of Venus in fetters, denoting the steadfastness that there must be in married people and lovers; this image also denotes the valour of the Lacedaemonian women against the Messenians, who were going to sack their city, which was valiantly defended by them.
blocks.pt: Венера вооружённая, Победительница и в оковах

blocks.text: Venus Victorious

Whether for this reason or for another, Venus was sometimes also called Victorious; and it is found that in a certain part of the Corinthian country there was a statue that held out a Victory in its hand and was therefore called Nikephoros, a Greek word, which among us means bearing Victory. And Pausanias writes that this was dedicated by Hypermnestra, after she was freed from the trial that her father Danaus had brought against her because she had not wished to obey him in killing her husband, as all her other sisters had done.

The Romans depicted Venus Victorious in this way, as is seen on a medal of the emperor Numerian. They painted and carved a most beautiful woman in a dress long to the ground, who with her right hand held out a small image of Victory, and in the left had a certain thing made in this fashion; some held that it represented the image which the people of Paphos worshipped under the name of Venus, as I have already said, and some others have held that it is rather a mirror, because Philostratus writes in the painting that he describes of the Cupids that the nymphs set up a statue to Venus, because she made them mothers of such beautiful offspring as the Cupids are, and dedicated to her a silver mirror, with some gilded ornaments for the feet.
Medal of Faustina

In another way too Venus is seen on an ancient medal of Faustina Augusta: with her left hand she holds a shield resting on the ground, which has two small figures carved in the middle, and with the right she holds out a Victory, and there are letters around that say, Venus Victorious. I remember having seen another medal, also ancient and also of Faustina, where there were letters that said, Venus, with a woman standing, dressed, who with her left hand held the hem of her dress on one side and pulled it up; with the other she held out something, I do not know what, which seemed to be an apple, perhaps in memory of the one that Paris gave her when he judged her more beautiful than Juno and Pallas.
Pausanias

So Pausanias too puts an apple in her hand when he reports a certain statue of Venus that was among the Sicyonians in Greece, saying that there was a temple dedicated to this goddess, into which never more than two women could enter; and of these, one, who had the keeping of it, always remained chaste and did not lie with her husband while she was in this office; the other had to be a virgin, because she handled the things of the sacrifices, and she did not remain in this charge for more than a year. And all the others who went to this temple to pray to the goddess for something stood outside, before the doors. Her statue was of gold, seated; with one hand it held some heads of poppy, and with the other an apple, and on the top of its head it had a certain thing that represents a pole, or let us say a hinge. And the one that was made by Tyndareus had a certain veil, such as the women of those times used to wear for adornment.
Morpho — Venus with her feet bound

Of this one the same Pausanias says that among the Lacedaemonians, above the temple of armed Venus, there was, as we should say, a chapel, where she sat; she was called Morpho there, with a certain veil on her head, as I said, and with cords or fetters (whichever they were) on her feet; it suffices that she had them bound, to show, as some say, that women must be of the firmest fidelity towards those to whom they are already bound by the marriage knot. But some others have said that Tyndareus made Venus thus in fetters to avenge himself for the adulteries committed by his daughters, as if this had come about through her fault.

Pausanias scoffs at this and does not wish to believe it, saying that it would be too foolish a thing to think that any harm could be done to Venus by making a statue of her out of cedar, like this one of which we are speaking, and putting fetters on her feet. And it seems to me that he speaks very well; for the ancients made the statues of the gods neither out of contempt nor out of any vengeance that they wished to take on them, but out of the reverence they bore them, for the help and favour they expected from them in all things, and sometimes also to show in their statues, to those who did not know it, their various powers. So, as can be seen on some other images too, the ancients put fetters on the feet not only of Venus but of the other gods as well, and not out of contempt nor out of vengeance but for other reasons, which I know I have given elsewhere, and so I do not repeat them.

But I say that although Venus seemed to be the chief numen of courtesans, as if she had once invented their art and put it into use, so that they celebrated her feast solemnly, praying her to give them grace, beauty and elegance, so that they might be loved by all, to their profit and gain, nevertheless she was also worshipped with no less devotion by honest girls, who thought that she could give them such charm and such good looks that it would then be easy for them to marry, because, as I have said at other times, the ancients gave Venus the care of marriage too.

Among the Greeks there was a certain cave, where, Pausanias writes, sacred honours were paid to Venus, and people went there for many reasons, but it seemed to be especially the custom for widows to go there, as they did, to pray the goddess to give them a second marriage happily. Married women likewise prayed to her, and not only there but also in her other temples, that she keep them always united with their husbands in mutual love and make them glad with new offspring and with a fair succession. So Venus was a numen common to all kinds of women, who, although perhaps more bound to this goddess than the others, acknowledged as coming from her almost all that happened to them happily, and men too thanked her for every benefit that had come from her.
Claudian

So, since the women all cut off their hair to make from it the ropes for hauling the machines that were then used in war, when the Romans, besieged by the Gauls on the Capitol, were in extreme need of everything, these, freed from the siege, dedicated, as Lactantius reports, a temple to Venus, where they depicted her Bald, and so named her in memory of what the women had done for the public benefit, though otherwise Venus is always depicted with most beautiful hair, as Claudian describes her, saying:

lines: Venus then on a fair gilded seat,
busy arranging her lovely blond hair,
had around her the Graces, of whom
one sprinkles with sweet nectar
the golden locks, and another
draws them out and loosens them with ivory teeth,
the third ties them in fair order
with a white hand and gathers them into lovely plaits.
blocks.author: Claudian

blocks.text: Bearded Venus

The ancients depicted her not only with hair but with a beard too: such a statue was worshipped in Cyprus as Venus, as Alexander ab Alexandro reports, which in face and aspect seemed a man, but then had about it women's garments. And Suda writes that the statue of Venus was made with a comb in the hand and a beard on the face because a certain illness once came upon the Roman women, so that all their hair fell out, as often happens in our times too, and they no longer had need to use a comb. For this reason the women, afflicted by so foul an illness, vowed themselves to Venus, and with endless vows begged her to provide for their misery; and she, who was always kind, accepting their devout prayers, brought it about that the women's hair no longer fell out, and what had fallen grew again.
All the gods male and female

As a sign of gratitude the women afterwards set up for her a statue that held a comb in its hand. And they gave her a beard too, so that this goddess might have the insignia of male and female, as one who presided over the universal generation of animals; and so from the middle upward they depicted her in the form of a male, and from the rest downward she was female. The ancients said this not only of Venus but of all the other gods too, giving each of them the name of both male and female, as though among them there were not the difference of sex that there is among mortals.

Image of Venus male and female, signifying that she presides over the universal generation of things, being taken for the air; and that among the gods there is no difference of sex, as among mortals; and image of Venus grieving for the death of Adonis, killed by the boar, understood as the wintry and cold season.
blocks.pt: Бородатая Венера и плач об Адонисе

blocks.text: Remarkable custom

We read that among the Carrhenians, a people of Arabia, this was observed: that all those who believed the Moon to be female and called her by a female name were under the women's rule and obliged to serve their wives; and on the contrary he who believed her male and so named her was never deceived by women, and his wife obeyed him and was subject to him, as duty seems to require.
The god Lunus

The Egyptians, although commonly they called the Moon by a female name, nevertheless in their mysteries called her not goddess but god. And for this reason the calf so celebrated among them was worshipped for her. And the Parthians worshipped the god Lunus, and Philochorus, who holds that Venus is one and the same as the Moon, as some of the Egyptians also believed — who for this reason made horns on her statue (because the Moon is depicted with horns, as can be seen in her image) — says that anciently men in women's dress used to sacrifice to her, and women dressed as men.

Not very different from this is what Seneca wrote in his *Natural Questions*, where he sets down that the Egyptians made two of each of the four elements established by them, one male and the other female. For they said that of the air the wind is the male, and the female is that which does not seem to move and is almost always misty; that the sea is the male of the waters, and fresh water is wholly female; that of fire that which burns is male, and female that which gives light and does no harm; and that of the earth the harder is male, such as stones and rocks, and female that which is softer and can be cultivated.
The Adonia

An idol of Venus was also made like the one that was seen on Mount Lebanon, which had a cloak about it that, beginning from the head, covered it all, and it seemed wholly sad and disconsolate, and with a hand likewise wrapped in the cloak it supported its drooping face, and, as Macrobius says, everyone who saw it believed that tears fell from its eyes. There Venus was shown so grieved for the death of Adonis, killed by a boar.

For this reason some days were kept as sacred, called the Adonia, and at that time the women everywhere in the cities laid certain images like dead bodies on little beds made for the purpose, and, as if they were persons only just dead, carried them weeping to the tombs; this, says Plutarch, they did in Athens in remembrance of the tears shed by Venus at the death of Adonis, her lover. And among the Argives, as Pausanias writes, the women went to weep for Adonis in a certain chapel not far from the temple of Jupiter Saviour.
Venus as half of the earth

This, if it is referred to the things of Nature, is thus interpreted by Macrobius: of the whole earth, this upper half, which is ours, was understood by the ancients under the name of Venus, and they called the other half, below, Proserpina. Besides this, of the twelve signs of the Zodiac, which surrounds it, six are called upper and the other six lower, these of winter, those of summer.
Adonis — the Sun

When, then, the Sun, who is signified by Adonis, goes in the time of summer through the six upper signs, Venus has her lover with her and is wholly glad. But then she is believed to weep and shows herself sad when she sees him descend, at the time of winter, into the lower signs, as if he were dying then, and Proserpina kept him for herself.
Adonis killed by the boar

And the fables said that a boar killed him because this animal seems to represent winter very well, seeing that it is covered all over with hard, rough bristles, likes to stay in muddy places, and feeds on acorns, which are fruits of winter; and winter is almost a mortal wound to the Sun, because it makes him shine for us for a very short time and gives us little of his heat. These two things death does, which deprives of light and of heat. Thus the image of Venus weeping under the cloak represents to us the earth in the time of winter, when it is for the most part covered with clouds and seems wholly afflicted because it does not see the Sun. Then the springs, which are the eyes of the earth, pour out abundant waters, and the fields, deprived of every adornment, show themselves all sad.
Interpretation of Venus
Marcus Tullius

Speaking of Venus in a natural sense, Eusebius too says that from her comes the power of generating, and that it is she who gives strength to the seed. They depict her in the form of a woman, to show that generation proceeds from her; they represent her as beautiful, because she is that star which, of all the others that are in Heaven, seems to be the most beautiful, called Hesperus in the evening, as Marcus Tullius says, and in the morning Lucifer.

Cupid stands at her side as a sign that from her is born every lascivious desire and every libidinous cupidity; her breasts and genitals are covered, because within the latter the seed is shut up, and in the former the nourishment of one who is already born of the conceived seed; and they say she was born of the sea because the water of the sea is believed to be hot and moist, and to move often, and when strongly agitated to make much foam, which things are all in the seed, since it is likewise white and foamy, and by its nature moist and hot.

Much else could be said of Venus by someone who wished to discuss her as a planet, and of the effects that come from her star, which adorns the third Heaven; from this one could also learn for what reason the ancients imagined that Mars, a god so terrible and fierce, stays so gently with her. But because this would divert me too much from my purpose of speaking about the images of the gods, not about their nature, I shall say no more of her, since I do not remember having read that the ancients depicted her in any other way. And it could well be that they did, but I do not know it, nor in writing can everything be set down so fully that something does not always remain, and it is right that it should, so that everyone may have something to say. It suffices that, by reading this little that I write, anyone who wishes to paint or carve the gods of the ancients will not lack a fairly good example; and he will also know why he does so.

I shall pass on, then, to speak of the company of Venus, which is the Graces and the Horae, as I have promised, but first putting down what Mars says while he holds this goddess in his arms, having taken amorous solace with her, when Jupiter commands him to go and stir up war for the kingdom of Thebes between Eteocles and Polynices, as Statius writes: from which, without saying more of it, one will be able to understand very well what and how great is the power of Venus; so that no one will have cause any longer to wonder when he sometimes sees the steadiest spirits and the firmest minds conquered by her, so that afterwards they have given themselves up as prey to amorous pleasures. These, then, are the words of Mars, rendered into the vernacular, with which I put an end to the image of Venus.

lines: O my sweet repose, kindly pleasure,
true peace of the troubled mind,
you can oppose me without ever fearing
me at all, even if I am angry;
you alone can curb and restrain
these steeds from their unbridled course
in fierce battles, and if it seems good to you,
you alone can disarm [?] these hands.
blocks.author: Statius
qm: “queste man puoi disamare” — “disamare” is not a normal verb; it is most likely a misprint for “disarmare” (“to disarm”), which fits the sense (Mars asks Venus to disarm his hands), and it is translated so.

blocks.text: Now that we have drawn Venus, mother of Cupid, whom we have likewise already portrayed, it is quite fitting that we speak of the Graces and the Horae together, who always go in company with her. For just as Venus and Cupid are the cause that new offspring keeps coming in succession, and that the human race is thereby preserved, so the Graces hold mortals gathered together, because the benefits that men do one another in turn are dear and pleasing, so that they stand joined together by the fair knot of friendship; without which there is no doubt at all that men would be far inferior to the other animals, and cities would become caves, or rather would not exist at all. For which reason it could almost be said that it would have been better for mortals not to be than, being, to live without the Graces.
Whose daughters the Graces are

But divine providence, which has care of the universe, wishes that these should nevertheless exist. According to some they were born of Venus and of Bacchus, and dwelt among mortals; which the fables invented, because it hardly seems that anything else is more pleasing to men than what comes from these gods; these I do not repeat, because they can be seen in the images of these gods. Others represent them as born in another way; but it is not for us to say this now, but only what statues they have had from the ancients, or how they have been painted.
Chrysippus

And although their names are different, the Graces and the Horae are nevertheless believed to be one and the same thing, but also to have different functions between them. And Chrysippus said that the Graces were a little younger than the Horae, and more beautiful too, and that for this reason the ancients gave them to Venus as companions.
The Horae are goddesses
Homer writes that the Horae are goddesses who stand at the gates of Heaven and keep guard there; and that it is their task to send the thick mist down upon mortals, and to take it away again.
Statius
Statius, describing the setting of the Sun, shows them coming quickly to take the bridles off the swiftest steeds, saying thus in our language:

lines: Then, when Phoebus has descended to the West,
he slackens the course for the burning steeds,
hiding himself beneath the Ocean,
the fair and lovely daughters of Nereus,
dwellers in the deep sea,
are about him; and with swift steps
to him at once come the ready Horae
to loose the reins from the foaming mouths
of the fierce horses, which they then send
to the green grass so that they may make good
the fatigue of the course already run,
and some of them strip off his locks,
which give light to the world with fair rays,
which adorn him in the form of a crown.
blocks.author: Statius

blocks.text: Eusebius
How many Horae there are

The Horae are nothing other than the seasons of the year; hence they are made out to be four, just as there are four parts of the year, so distinguished by the Sun and likewise named from him, because among the Egyptians the Sun, besides many other names that he had there, was also called Horus. On this Eusebius writes of them in this way. The Horae, whom they say to be the four seasons of the year and to open and shut the gates of Heaven, are given now to the Sun and now to Ceres, and for this reason they carry two baskets, one of flowers, by which spring is shown, the other full of ears of grain, which signifies summer.
Ovid

And Ovid likewise says in the *Fasti* that these stand in company with Janus on guard at the gates of Heaven; and when he afterwards tells of Flora, in whose power are the flowering meadows, he says that the Horae, dressed in the thinnest veils, come into these at times to gather various flowers, to make fair wreaths of them for themselves.
Pausanias

And Pausanias writes that the ancients placed them on the head of Jupiter, together with the Parcae, wishing perhaps to show in this way that Fate is nothing other than the will of God, from which also come the changes of the times. But I have now said more about the nature of the Horae than is needed to know how they are to be painted. Coming to this, then, I shall give only one portrait of them, as Philostratus paints it in a fine picture, saying that the Horae, having come down to earth, go turning the year (which is in the form of a certain round thing) with their hands; from which turning it comes about that the earth then produces, year after year, everything that is born; and they are blond, dressed in the thinnest veils, and walk over the dry ears of grain so lightly that they break none, nor bend even one; they are pleasant and joyful in aspect; they sing most sweetly; in turning that orb, or ball, or circle, whichever it may be, they seem to give marvellous delight to those who look on; and they go as if leaping almost always, often raising their fair arms on high; they have their blond hair scattered over their shoulders, their cheeks rosy, like one who already feels warmed from running, and their eyes bright and quick in movement.

Image of the Horae, also called Graces by some, and of Apollo, the former understood as the four seasons of the year, the latter as the Sun that varies the seasons; held also to be goddesses of friendship, beauty, charm and amiability, goddesses of cheerfulness, play and pleasure; they also denote God's mercy toward the guilty.
Four Graces

Since these, then, bring it about that the earth returns to us the sown grain and the other fruits with great interest, as though, showing herself grateful for what we give her, she rewarded us in this way, it was said that the Graces were four, because there are as many seasons of the year, called Horae, as I have said, meaning to signify that these and the Graces are the same. They were therefore represented with wreaths on their heads, and one had hers of flowers, and another of ears of grain; the third of grapes and vine leaves, and the last of olive. And the ancients feigned that Apollo had them in his right hand, because the diversity of the seasons comes from the Sun.
Diodorus
Why the Graces are companions of Venus

And since, as Diodorus says, they were worshipped by the ancients because they thought that they could give beauty of face and of all the other parts of the body, with that charm which so delights at times whoever looks at them, they were for that reason placed in the company of Venus. And it was also their task to bring it about that men should not be ungrateful to one another, but should repay with a cheerful heart the benefits received.
Two Graces

For which reason some said that the Graces were two, and among the Lacedaemonians they worshipped only two, as Pausanias writes, because it seems that likewise there are only two effects that come from them: the one, to do a benefit to another; the other, to repay the benefits received.
Three Graces

But the same Pausanias also says afterwards that all those who placed the Graces at Delos with the statues of Mercury, Bacchus and Apollo represented them as three, and that there were likewise three at the entrance to the citadel of Athens. Hence it has since always been commonly held that they are three, because a benefit ought not to be returned such as we received it, but much greater, and often doubled. From this it comes that one of them stands with her back toward us, and two look at us, giving us to understand thereby that in returning the good done to us we must be much more liberal than when we are the first to do a benefit to another; which, however, ought not to be done in expectation of reward, because whoever does this may be called a usurer rather than a liberal benefactor.
The Graces are virgins, glad

It is said that the Graces are young virgins, glad and smiling, to show that whoever does a benefit must use no deceit at all, but do it with a sincere and cheerful heart. This will be better understood also by whoever notes that they were represented naked and loosed from every knot, as Horace sang of them, because men must be with one another of a free mind, loosed from all deceit, naked and open.

Images of the three Graces, goddesses of beauty and grace; goddesses also of gratitude and benefit, named Euphrosyne or joyfulness, Aglaia or charm, Thalia or pleasantness; goddesses of conversation, sociability and friendship, and of that cheerful life which men desire to live.
Eteocles

Pausanias, though, writes that he never found out who was the first to represent the Graces naked, because from the beginning everyone represented them clothed, and that he does not know for what reason their attire was afterwards changed, so that all have represented them naked, both the painters and the sculptors. Besides this he states [?] that Eteocles of Boeotia was the first to ordain that the Graces should be worshipped and should be three, but he does not know what names he gave them.
qm: “Oltre di ciò mette, Ethocle di Beotia fosse il primo, che ordinasse …” — the construction is defective (“mette” is followed by no “che”; the sentence is evidently elliptical, and the verb is perhaps “mette [in scritto]”, “sets down”); translated “he states that Eteocles … was the first to ordain”.

blocks.text: Names of the Graces: Euphrosyne, Aglaia, Thalia. Pasithea

So we now name them as they were named by Hesiod, who called one of them Euphrosyne, which means cheerfulness and joyfulness, the other Aglaia, which signifies majesty and charm, the third Thalia, which comes to mean pleasantness. And Homer called one of them Pasithea, the one whom Juno promises to give as wife to Sleep, if he goes to Jupiter and puts him to sleep; and he also calls one of them Grace, by a proper name, who he says was the wife of Vulcan and stayed with him always. She, with fair veils on her head, comes to meet Tethys when she goes to beg Vulcan that he be willing to give arms to Achilles, her son.

In Greece, among the Eleans, the Graces had a temple, in which their statues were of wood with gilded garments, and they had the face and the hands and the feet of white ivory. One of them had a rose in her hand, another a certain thing made like a die; the third a sprig of myrtle. And of these things they give this reason. The rose and the myrtle belong to Venus, and were therefore given to those who for the most part are with her; and that square thing signifies the games that the innocent young virgins play among themselves, to their own pleasure and to that of whoever sees them; which does not happen with women of greater age, to whom more serious things are fitting, not games. All this Pausanias says.

But of the three emblems of the Graces others give another reason, and say that the rose signifies their pleasantness; the die, that they must go and return in turn, as dice go when one plays with them; and the myrtle, that they must always be green and never wither, as this plant is always green.
Alexander ab Alexandro. Aristotle

And as Alexander ab Alexandro reports, and Aristotle wrote before him in the *Moral Writings*, the ancients used to build the temple of the Graces in the middle of the squares, so that willingly serving another and repaying the benefits received should be before everyone's eyes, because this is the proper office of the Graces.

This, however, ought not to be done without good consideration, because it is a poor thing to give thus to one who does not deserve it or has no need of it, rather than to one who has need of it and deserves that it be given to him [?]. This too the ancients taught us likewise in the image of the Graces, depicting Mercury as their escort and leader, who represents reason and sound discourse, so that, following in the footsteps of reason, men may know how, and when, and to whom they are to give and do a benefit, imitating, as far as they can, the divine goodness, which is always ready to do good.
qm: “perche così è mal dare a chi non merita, ò non ne hà cui fa dibisogno, & merita, che gli sia dato” — the sentence is garbled (after “non ne hà” something is missing, probably “bisogno, che [dare] a cui …” or “che a cui”; “cui” is left without a governing word). Translated by sense, supplying “rather than” between the two persons, as the contrast requires.

blocks.text: Image of the Graces guided by Mercury, denoting that helping and beneficence must be done with reason, at the right time, and to the deserving, without hope of reward, with a sincere heart, and that the one benefited must, when occasion offers, return the benefit, if not in deeds then at least in words.

Hence, says Macrobius, the ancients placed the Graces in Apollo's right hand, and the bow with the arrows in his left, to give us to understand that the divine hand is much readier to do good than harm, and, as long as it can (that is, as long as it is not forced by our wicked conduct, because then it uses what it holds in the left hand, to punish us), is a generous giver of its favours to mortals.

And men too must do this, learning it, if they do not otherwise know it, from the image of the Graces, which Seneca explains very well where he writes of doing a benefit to another, saying that these are three, because one does the benefit, another receives it, and the third gives the return for it. Or else that one does, another returns, the third does and returns; so that there come to be three ways of doing a benefit.

They stand with their hands and arms joined together, because the order of doing good to another is that it should pass from hand to hand and return also to the profit of the one who first did it, and in this way the pleasing knot of friendship holds men joined together. They are cheerful and joyful in aspect, because such must whoever does a benefit to another show himself, and such for the most part are those who receive it. They are young, because the memory of benefits received must never grow old.

They are virgins, because in doing good to another it must be done with a pure and sincere heart, and without any knot of obligation; as their ungirt and loose garments also show, which are bright and transparent, because the heart of the one who does a benefit must be within such as it shows itself outside in deeds, and because whoever receives the benefit must not hide it, but make it seen by everyone. For this too is a gratitude: when the benefit received cannot be repaid in deeds, to acknowledge it at least in words, and to make the liberality of the benefactor plain to all.
And here let the image of the Graces end, with a sculpture of these that is seen in Rome in the Colonna house, with Latin verses, which in the vernacular mean this:

lines: Truly these are the naked Graces, who once were
made of white marble, polished and fair;
all three have among themselves a like face,
so that you can know them for sisters;
all three are equal in age, and beauty
is likewise seen equal in all three.
Thalia stands with her face turned to her sisters
and joins and knots her arms
with theirs, who are on the left
and on the right, looking at us,
this one is named Euphrosyne, that one Aglaia;
with pleasing knots of fair arms
they are entwined together with the third sister.
Jupiter is their father, and from heavenly seed
they were conceived by their mother Eunomia,
who afterwards with a happy birth
brought them forth into the world as joyful and pleasing handmaids
to gracious Cytherea, so that through them
she often, together with fair Cupid,
increases amorous pleasures in such a way
that every gentle heart is left conquered by them.

blocks.text: THE END.
Annotations of Lorenzo Pignoria on the Book of Cartari's Images.
Fol. 2, line 3.

That no light of religion was ever attributed by anyone to animals is not wholly true. For the Egyptians said great things about their sacred animals, such as the cynocephalus, the scarab, and others. On this see Horapollo, and our Commentary on the Hieroglyphic Table, which once belonged to Cardinal Bembo, of glorious memory, and is now to be seen in the Gallery of His Most Serene Highness the Duke of Mantua. Indeed, particular things of great wonder are told of elephants. And read Aelian in Book 7 of the *History of Animals*, at chapter 39, and in Book 4, at chapter 9; Pliny in Book 8, at chapter 1. Among the moderns, Porcacchi on Sannazaro's *Arcadia*, at fol. 174 of the Pavia edition of 1596.
Line 14.

The Latins call God DEVS, which without doubt comes from the Greek word ΖΕΥΣ (Zeus), changing the Z to D, as has been the custom in all languages, on the testimony of Claudius Mitalerius on Valerius Maximus. Some others hold that it derives from the Greek word ΔΕΣ [?], which means fear; hence Petronius Arbiter said:
qm: The Greek word is printed in the book without diacritical marks and in a corrupted form; by the sense the word means “fear”.

lines: Fear first made gods in the world.
blocks.author: Petronius Arbiter

blocks.text: Lactantius Placidus, commentator on Statius Papinius, was of this opinion, in Book 3 of the *Thebaid*, at verse 661, where he cites Lucan and Mintanor the musician, who is reported also by Fulgentius in the first book of the *Mythologies*. Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux in France, alludes to this view in the sermon he delivered at the Council of Tours, and he confirms it with the verse of Psalm LX:

lines: You have given an inheritance to those who fear your name, O Lord.
blocks.author: Psalm LX

blocks.text: Diogenes Laertius writes some fine things about the name of God in the life of Zeno, near the end.
Fol. 3, line 18.

This senate of twelve of the great gods is read in two verses of Ennius in Martianus Capella, in the first book of the *Marriage of Philologia and Mercury*. Indeed, antiquity had so apportioned them that one fell to each month, as is plainly seen in the Rustic Calendar published and explained by Fulvio Orsini, a most exquisite observer of ancient curiosities. See Macrobius in Book 1 of the *Saturnalia*, at chapter 12, and the *Sacred Fasti* of Ambrosius Novidius, who with a praiseworthy invention has striven to correct the superstition of the ancients.
Fol. 5, line 10.
Lucan does not say that the people of Marseilles paid reverence to tall trunks, and that there were no idols in the woods. Let his verses be the witness:

lines: — but barbarous in ritual
were the sacred rites of the gods, altars set up on dreadful altar-tops.
blocks.author: Lucan

blocks.text: Here are the altars. Further down:

lines: — then abundant water falls from black
springs, and the mournful idols of the gods
lack art and stand shapeless on hewn trunks.
blocks.author: Lucan

blocks.text: Here are the statues. But there is no man who does not err.
Fol. 9, line 39.

On the respect paid to statues see Dio Chrysostom in the oration he made to the people of Rhodes, in which he censures the abuse of removing the name from the statues of men of the past and putting another on them. Moreover, read Cassiodorus in Book 7 of the *Variae*, at formulas 13 and 14, where he says that in Rome there was another people of statues; and it must indeed have been so, because although the galleries of princes and of private persons, in Italy and outside Italy, have been adorned with the statues of Rome, the vein is still not exhausted, and every day they are found in such quantity. Let whoever wishes see Justus Lipsius in Book 3 of *On the Greatness of Rome*, at chapter 9, and the Incruscato in his *Compendium*.
Fol. 15, line 39.

Statius speaks of Demogorgon in Book 4 of the *Thebaid*, according to the exposition of Lactantius Placidus, an ancient grammarian; and see Mazzoni on Dante, in Book 1, at chapter 63. And perhaps it was to Demogorgon that the sorceress Erichtho wished to allude, in Lucan in Book 6.
Fol. 17, line 7.

Some who have sought the reason for this adjective “eternal” (*eterno*) have said that it comes from *eui terno*, as Varro does in Book 5 of *On the Latin Language*. Others have held that it derives from the ether (*etere*), as Isidore attests of some in Book 7 of his *Origins*. I would say with Varro that it has its origin in the Age (*Euo*), which Arnobius in Book III of *Against the Gentiles* calls *Euità*. Censorinus describes it in the book *On the Birthday*, at chapter 16 (I cite the edition of Ludovicus Carrio), as immense, without origin and without end, which always was and always will be in the same manner. On Eternity, whoever wishes to see some refined thought should read Antonio Agostini in the 2nd *Dialogue on Medals*.
Fol. 25, line 39.

Theophrastus in the *Characters* writes that the superstitious man, coming upon the anointed stones that are found where three roads meet, will anoint them, and will not depart before he has knelt down before them. On this passage see what Casaubon writes. Lucian too touches on this custom in *The False Prophet*, saying that that swindler, wherever he caught sight of a stone, anointed or wreathed, at once knelt down. It is read in the *Apology* of Apuleius, in the one they call the first, and in Prudentius, in the second book against Symmachus.

A similar point is touched on by the Capitulary of Charlemagne, in the first book, at chapter 64, where it says that some madmen kindled lights to trees, stones and springs. And in the same Capitulary (in the imperfect one, however, that goes about under the name of Laws of the Lombards) is seen a law of King Liutprand that forbids the worship of springs, or of the tree that the peasants call Holy. It is in Book 2, at title 37. See Carolus Paschalius in the book *On Wreaths*, Book 4, chapter 4; Pliny the Younger, Book 8, letter 8; Seneca, letter 41; Justus Lipsius on the 14th book of Tacitus's *Annals*.
Fol. 29, line 8.

Martianus Capella does not say that Saturn had, as an ornament of the head, now a serpent, now a lion's head, and now a boar's; but that he seemed now to have the face of a dragon, now of a lion, now of a boar, and so people have sought to represent him. And of these faces I could say nothing else, except that Martianus had an eye to the malignity of the influences of this planet, which, as Natale Conti writes in Book 2 of the *Mythology*, at chapter 2, inclines men to be melancholic, envious, malicious, proud, avaricious, and tenacious in anger.
Fol. 31, last line.

Homer speaks of the Prayers in Book 10 of the *Iliad*, in Phoenix's admonition to Achilles. And Andrea Alciato made a most beautiful emblem of it, which is the hundred and thirtieth. And from Homer's Prayers (*Lite*) perhaps the Latin verb *litare* has its origin, which means to obtain by entreaty, as is read in Nonius Marcellus; although Varro derives it from *luere*, which is to pay, as can be seen in the same grammarian; and Hadrianus Turnebus reports it in Book 18, at chapter 20. But in favour of my opinion stands the authority of Festus.
Fol. 34, line 12.

Whoever wishes to see exactly this manner of counting on the fingers cannot come upon a better book than that of Bede cited by the Author. But note that the corrected edition of that little book is that of Elias Vinetus; the others will be defective. And the ancient authors are full of this custom of reckoning. Suetonius in the life of the Emperor Claudius, at chapter 21; Quintilian in Book XI of his *Institutes*, at chapter 3; Pliny in Book 34, at chapters 7 and 8; Seneca in letter 88, and in Book 3 *On Anger*, at chapter 33; Aelian in Book 6 of the *History of Animals*, at chapter 57; Martianus Capella in Book 7 of the *Marriage*, etc., right at the beginning; Symposius in Riddle 100; Aristides in the 2nd of the *Sacred Discourses*, and many others.
Fol. 36.

The first images of the Seasons are taken from the gold medal of Antoninus Caracalla in Sebastiano Erizzo, and from another, of the Emperor Diocletian, which was to be seen in the study of the late Signor Lelio Pasqualini. The second are according to the Author's own idea, except that in the place of Vulcan and Aeolus, Vesta has been put.
Fol. 37, line 27.

What the Author calls a Temple is seen in Rome, near the church of St George, in the Forum Boarium. Bartolomeo Marliani had it drawn in his book, Book 3, chapter 14, and so did Antonio Agostini in Dialogue 4 on Medals, who calls it an Arch, and rightly in my opinion. See Suetonius in the life of Augustus, at chapter 31, and on Suetonius, Livinus Torrentius, bishop of Antwerp, and Casaubon. And our Author himself, a little further down, calls triumphal arches Jani. But whoever wishes fuller information about Janus should read Barnabas Brissonius in Book 1 of the *Formulae*.
Fol. 43.

Of the two images of Hebe, one has been taken from the medal of the Emperor M. Aurelius; the other has been represented in the dress of the ancient cupbearers, as can be seen in my book on the offices of slaves among the ancients. On the same medal “Juventas” is read, who among the Latins is the one who among the Greeks is Hebe. See Lambinus on ode 30 of the first book of Horace, and Servius on the 1st book of the *Aeneid*.
Fol. 46, line 26.
Whoever wishes more on the Muses should see Goffredo Liuocerio in a refined little book of his, printed with the *Mythology* of Natale Conti.
Fol. 52, line 28.

The text of Martianus Capella is corrupt, as I have already shown in my Exposition of the Hieroglyphic Table, which is now to be seen in the Gallery of His Most Serene Highness of Mantua. For it must be understood that on the ship seven brothers german stood at the helm. That on its prow there is seen the figure of a cat; of a lion on the mast; of a crocodile on the outside. See the text; for the correction is clear.
Fol. 53.

The figure of Apollo and Daphne has been taken from a most beautiful cameo that belonged to Monsignor Grimani, Patriarch of Aquileia, of most honoured memory; and on the laurel one can read Natale Conti in the *Mythology*, and Ammianus Marcellinus in Book 29.
Fol. 60, line 33.

In Rome in the year 1606 I saw a large piece of marble in the square of the Capitol that represented a grotto of Mithraic things, but much damaged and worn. In its substance it bore a great similarity to the figure that has been represented above. On the belly of the bull these words were read: “To the god Sun, the Unconquered, Mithras”; at the bottom of the neck it had these carved: “Nama Sebesio”; at the bottom of the right thigh: “Amycus Seronensis”. There were two figures standing, one on each side, but ruined; and above the grotto a quadriga of the Sun and a biga of the Moon. And I have thought at times that this large piece of marble was one of the remains of paganism, whose ruin was brought about by that Gracchus of whom St Jerome makes mention in writing to Laeta, and Prudentius at the end of Book 1 against Symmachus. The words of St Jerome are:

lines: A few years ago your kinsman Gracchus, whose name sounded of patrician nobility, when he held the urban prefecture, did he not overturn, break and burn the Cave of Mithras and all the monstrous idols by which the Raven, Misus, Meles (so Martianus Victorius reads), the Lion, Perses, Helios, Bromius, the Father are initiated?
blocks.author: St Jerome

blocks.text: And to the purpose of these names recalled by St Jerome, a passage of Porphyry in Book 4 of *On Abstinence* works marvellously, where he relates that in the mysteries of Mithras the men were called lions, the women lionesses, others ravens, some eagles, and certain ones hawks.

In the antiquities of Rome, printed some time ago and put together in a quite large volume, one of these images of Mithraic things was to be seen, which someone, I do not know who, has explained and reported as a portrait of Agriculture, but out of place in my opinion.
Fol. 63.

Beside the image of Apollo is seen the ox Apis, taken from a medal of Julian the Apostate, who, as Ammianus Marcellinus reports in Book 22, had this beast diligently sought out. And whoever wishes more on it, let him see my exposition of the Isiac Table.
Fol. 66.

From two ancient intaglios we have taken the images of Serapis and Isis that are seen here; on which whoever wishes more should read the first chapter of the Isiac Table, and see at the end of the same book certain drawings of ancient figures that belonged to Signor Lelio Pasqualini.
Fol. 70.

The figure of Aesculapius, which is seen small on a cameo, is taken from the medal of the Emperor M. Antoninus Caracalla, and is like an ancient statue that I saw in Rome eight years ago, in the house of the Signori Massimi, at the Valle. But it must be noted that the engraver, in this one of ours, not understanding Aesculapius's hair, has made him a Janus.
Fol. 71, line 17.

Peter Apian (if I am not mistaken) was notably deceived in this figure of Aesculapius. For if it is an ancient thing, which from the garments seems to me not to be, I would say that it was rather either the goddess Copia or one of the seasons of the year. Nor will it seem strange to anyone that I give this note on Apian; for Antonio Agostini too, in his Dialogue 11, says that the said author's book is full of feigned ancient inscriptions.
Fol. 77.

In the cameo Providence has been represented, as she is figured on a medal of the Emperor Antoninus Pius, which I have. And it is clearly seen that whoever shaped her wished to say that the Providence of the Emperor is the salvation of the world.
Fol. 79.

This figure has been taken from the cameos of the Most Reverend Patriarch Grimani. And on the subject of Aesculapius's daughters it is to be noted that he had four, as many as Aristides names in the oration he composed in praise of Podalirius and Machaon, sons of Aesculapius. And they are Iaso, Aegle, Hygieia, and Panacea. And I remember seeing an ancient copper medal on which a serpent came out of an altar, and beneath it was written Iaso.
Fol. 95, at the end.

In the study of the Most Illustrious Signor Federico Contarini, Procurator of St Mark, of glorious memory, there was to be seen a most beautiful ancient carnelian in which, with Cupid looking on, Apollo wrote in a flower these characters I A, and in the flower was inserted a most beautiful youth as far as the navel, who with open arms seemed to lament his misery. See the fable in Ovid in Book 10 of the *Metamorphoses*, who holds that A I A I was written in the flower, against the authority of our sculpture, which, enlarged, is the one that follows.
See Servius on the third eclogue of Virgil, and Probus at the same place; Palaephatus, and Philostratus, the elder and the younger, in the *Imagines*.

Nor less celebrated among writers is the victory that Apollo won over Marsyas, set out in the figures written below, taken from the antique, where in one cameo Marsyas is seen playing the pipes, on which see Apuleius in the first book of the *Florida*; and in another the same victory of Apollo. On which Apollodorus relates that Apollo made a show of his skill with the cithara played backwards, and commanded Marsyas to do the same with the flutes, and since Marsyas did not succeed, he left his skin there.

We shall seal this chapter with the figure of Lucifer, companion of the Dawn, which I once saw on an ancient carnelian by a skilled master, in which, however, I do not see observed the rule of Lactantius Placidus, on the sixth book of Statius's *Thebaid*, namely that his chariot is drawn by a single horse. For he says that the poets give four horses to the Sun, two to the Moon, a single one to the stars. It is quite true that the engraver of the gem may not have been a poet.
Fol. 94, line 10.

To show this uniformity of Juno and Diana, beside the image of Lucina the portrait of Juno Lucina, taken from ancient medals, has been placed. But on this subject one should note what Martin Delrio writes on chapter 14 of Genesis; namely that the city of Astaroth Carnaim received this name from an idol of Juno or Diana with two horns, which was worshipped in that city. And whoever reads the theologians of paganism will not judge this exchange strange, since in the same writers greater follies are read about these masquerades, especially according to the custom of the Orientals. And I have touched on something of this in my exposition on the Table of Isis. But who knows whether this two-horned Astarte was not Isis;

I for my part believe it. Nor does the name of Astarte give me trouble, because perhaps the Hebrews applied it to all the female deities, in the way that Baal, or Beel, was applied to all the males. The true interpretation, however, of Astaroth Carnaim I think can be drawn from what Eusebius writes in Book 1 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, in the last chapter, namely that Astarte, wife of Heaven, made for herself on her head, as an adornment, a pair of horns. The image found in the time of Pope Leo X will be the one set below.
Fol. 104, line 9.
This imperial hecatomb is related by Julius Capitolinus in the life of the Emperors Maximus and Balbinus.
Fol. 106, line 7.

Whether [?] the emperors could have had a shortage of these real animals I would not dare to imagine, for since they were masters of the world, what wonder will it be if they had them in hundreds? That Democares, of whom Apuleius makes mention in Book 4 of the *Golden Ass*, had no few animals for the games that he had to put on. Pompey the Great, as Dio writes, at the dedication of his theatre had 500 lions killed. These men did not yet have the means that the emperors afterwards had of gathering together so many beasts. See Suetonius in the Life of Titus, at chapter 7; Claudian in the 3rd Panegyric on Stilicho; and among the moderns Julius Caesar Bulengerus in his treatise *On Hunting*. But I believe that our Author is speaking of the poor, as he seems to declare further on.
qm: There is a misprint in this word in the book; by the sense it is “could”; translated “Whether … could”.

blocks.text: Fol. 107, line 5.

Nicolas Remy, privy councillor of the Highnesses of Lorraine, has composed three fine and curious books with the title *Demonolatry*, in which, from trials lawfully conducted against wizards and witches, he goes on to show the diabolical tyranny over those wretches who have done homage with their souls to the enemy of souls. Now in Book 1, at chapter 7, at the end, he shows that Empusa and Hecate are demons, who, among the ancients too, were accustomed to appear both by night and at midday, especially when sacrifice was made for the souls of the dead. And to this view he fits the verse of Psalm XC:

lines: from the arrow flying by day, from the business walking in darkness; from onslaught and the noonday demon.
blocks.author: Psalm XC

blocks.text: The same author, in chapter 23 of the same book, goes on to relate in what shapes the demon transforms himself when he wishes to be seen by someone: now into a dog, now into a horse, now into a fly, now into a cat; and many times in human form, though dressed in black and in a long garment, at the first meetings, so as not to frighten with the monstrosity of the feet, which he has inseparably. And I have heard tell from a trustworthy person how in Padua he appeared to a poor man so dressed; but that from beneath the hem of the garment claws were seen like those of an eagle, or of another bird of prey.

Martin Delrio also discusses Hecate in his *Magical Disquisitions*, Book 2, question 27, section 2, and describes her in exactly the manner in which she is seen portrayed in many ancient memorials, in gems and various stones for rings and for what the ancients called amulets. And note that Diana of Ephesus too was represented thus, and is seen in the cameos at fol. 109 and 91 and continually on ancient medals, and Minucius Felix makes mention of it in the *Octavius* with these words:

lines: Diana meanwhile is a huntress with her dress girt high, and the Ephesian, heaped with many breasts and udders, and Trivia, dreadful with three heads and many hands.
blocks.author: Minucius Felix

blocks.text: And these last words explain the cameos that have been placed at fol. 104. But this figure has great conformity with Isis giving milk to Horus, as is seen on an ancient carnelian and elsewhere.

In the cameo Isis has been represented as she is seen on the ancient medals of Hadrian and Antoninus Pius. It is quite true that the draughtsman forgot to put in her hand the sistrum, which is clearly seen on them. And this figure, in my judgement, signifies the Ship of Isis, which is mentioned in the ancient Rustic Calendar. And on the medal of Antoninus there is seen a port lighthouse, which confirms the conjecture all the more. Read Apuleius in Book 11.
Fol. 108, line 12.

The Author calls the sistrum a cymbal, and he is mistaken, because these two instruments were very different from each other, as can be seen in my Commentary on Slaves, at fol. 88 and 91. And a similar licence is seen in Antonio Agostini (if, however, the translator is not to blame for it), who calls the tympanum by the name of crotalum.
Fol. 110, last line.

Martianus Capella, cited by the Author, makes no mention of cymbals, but of Nilotic sistra. What a sistrum was is seen in the preceding image; and it is seen figured in our book on slaves at fol. 88. Nor was it a crotalum, as Joseph Scaliger holds, but very different. Nor was the tympanum otherwise a crotalum, as Antonio Agostini wrote in the second and fifth dialogue (unless we wish to say that this was an error of the translator). A most beautiful ancient sistrum, quite whole, was formerly to be seen in the hands of Monsignor Mocenico, Bishop of Nona. And perhaps Michele Mercati in his book on the obelisks of Rome, at chapter XI, fol. 120, where he mentions half-circles of gold and silver that are seen with hieroglyphic figures, understood nothing other than sistra, since sistra were made both of gold and of silver, as one also reads in Apuleius in Book XI of the *Golden Ass*.
Fol. 112, at the end.

Philostratus writes in the *Imagines* that in Athens the Dragon of Pallas, which until then had its dwelling in the citadel of that city, loved the Athenians for their gold; since they used it to make an ornament for the head, with figures of golden cicadas. Isidore in Book 19 of the *Origins*, at chapter 30, means the same, although the rest, being corrupt, has *Cyclades* for *Cicadas*. Gregory of Nazianzus touches on the same usage in writing to Nicobulus.
Fol. 113, line 30.

The Egyptians in ancient times made great account of the lotus, and of its flower in particular, since in the Isiac Table expounded by me the flower is seen in many places. And in my said book I have noted something about it. And in particular that the Basilidian heretics of antiquity, so called from Basilides of Alexandria, who lived around the year of the Lord 124, very frequently had the flower of the lotus engraved on their monstrous seals, upon which Harpocrates sits. And in my above-cited book six drawings of them are seen, in the last plate of the five placed at the end.

In the cameo (as the painters say) the image of Jupiter the rain-bringer and thunderer has been figured; taken from the Antonine Column, in the sculpture of which paganism, so as not to give the honour of the Marcomannic victory to the Christians, had Jupiter represented in the manner seen in the air, pouring water, hail and lightning bolts upon the barbarians. But the truth of the history is seen in Onofrio Panvinio, in Book 2 of his *Fasti*, and in Cardinal Baronio, in vol. 2 of the *Ecclesiastical Annals*.
Fol. 123, line 38.

In ancient monuments, that is in gems and in marbles, satyrs of two kinds are seen: some with the thighs and legs of a goat; some with a wholly human form, except that they have behind a small tail and the ears of a beast. We have had both kinds portrayed here on a little tablet.
Fol. 114, line 36.

Whether they were truly satyrs or not, there is much to be said. And besides what Cartari writes of them, one should read Casaubon in his books *On Satire*, in Book 1, chapter 2, where there is a collection of observations on a similar subject. And this author narrates that not many years ago there was brought before King Henry IV of France, of glorious memory, a certain man who worked as a charcoal-burner and who, at seven years of his age, began to put out a horn on his head, and some other particulars worthy of consideration. And by all means see St Jerome in the Life of St Anthony the Abbot, and Plutarch in the Life of Sulla, cited by Cartari himself, in which I do not know how to doubt, as Casaubon seems to be hinting. The case of the French charcoal-burner was in 1595, and the author of the *Chronicum Chronicorum* notes it, in Book 2.
Pliny, describing the painting of Philoxenus of Eretria, does not say that he painted three satyrs who with cups in their hands drank deeply; but that three Sileni were eating together.
Fol. 135, line 5.

Honour was figured by antiquity as both male and female. Male on this marble and on a medal of the Emperor M. Aurelius the Philosopher. Female on the medals of Galba, Vitellius and Vespasian. Whoever made it male perhaps had regard to the conception that men generally form of it, among whom great account is made of it. Whoever made it female, to its substance, because it is the shadow of Virtue. See the Author at fol. 330.
Fol. 135, line 32.

Because many among the ancients could not decide well whether the horn of plenty was Achelous's or that of the goat Amalthea, in an ancient gem, the drawing of which we record below, the goddess Copia sits with two poppies in her hand, upon the shoulders of a goat and of a bull. Beside this there is another, with a nymph who adorns the horn with flowers and fruits, as is read in Ovid, if I am not mistaken. The principal figure, then, is taken from an ancient medal of Trajan that is mine, very well preserved; in which is clearly seen what Antonio Agostini noted in his 2nd Dialogue, namely that in the middle of the horn the point of the ploughshare is seen. And all this was done to give it to be understood that the cultivated earth is what produces abundance, or Copia, as we may say.

figs.pt: Честь в мужском и женском образе

blocks.text: Fol. 137, line 14.
On Jupiter worshipped at Terracina see Stephanus Pighius, in the *Hercules Prodicius*, at fol. 433, and together with him Vincenzo Mirabella on the third medal of Syracuse.
Fol. 143, line 1.

The Author notes that the thunderbolt was never given to Minerva, neither in statue nor in painting. Which, however, is not very true. And we see on the medals of the Emperor Domitian the thunderbolt in the hand of Minerva on more than one of them: as, for example, in the *Twelve Caesars* of Enea Vico, in copper on plate 2 at no. 22, in silver on plate 2 at no. 24. And Antonio Agostini touches on it in Dialogue 5.
And Domitian perhaps had regard to the verses of Virgil:

lines: — Could Pallas not burn up the fleet
of the Argives and sink the men themselves in the sea
for the guilt and the furies of one man, Ajax son of Oileus?
She herself, hurling from the clouds the swift fire of Jupiter,
scattered the ships and overturned the waters with winds.
blocks.author: Virgil

blocks.text: And of this violence of Ajax Oileus, Antonio Agostini gives a drawing taken from a rather beautiful ancient marble.
Of this Ajax a fine account is read in Philostratus in his *Heroes*, and in Book 2 of the *Imagines*; and see the painting of Polygnotus described by Pausanias in Book 10.
Fol. 145, line 14.

The Author's not having understood well the words of Quintus Curtius has caused all the figures that up to now represent in this book the idol of Jupiter Ammon to have turned out false. Quintus Curtius in Book 4 writes thus:

lines: That thing which is worshipped as a god in this place is not like the figures that craftsmen commonly form of the deities. Up to the navel it is like a ram, and is composed of emeralds and gems.
blocks.author: Quintus Curtius

blocks.text: Thus it ought to have been represented. But on account of the difficulty of getting the draughtsman, and the tedium (be it permitted to confess it) suffered in so long an undertaking, which turned out harder than was at first estimated, it was thought enough to advise the reader of what had to be done, leaving the care to whoever will, of forming the image in conformity with the truth [?]. And that Ammon and Serapis were not different from Jupiter was the thought of the person who had the ring gem engraved that we have represented in the preceding figure.
qm: In the book the sentence repeats the same verb twice in a row with no evident connection; translated according to the general sense.

blocks.text: Fol. 147, line 27.

That Jupiter was wreathed with olive was noted also by Carolus Paschalius in his *Wreaths*, and he proves it with the authority of Cornutus and perhaps of Sophocles. But the same author warns that antiquity gave Jupiter three kinds of wreath: of flowers, of leaves, of metals; and in another place he cites Tertullian, who reports on the testimony of Diodorus that Jupiter was the first to use a wreath: and this after the victory over the Titans.
Fol. 154, line 36.

Iris was messenger not only of Juno but of the other gods too, as Lactantius Placidus notes in Book 2 of Statius's *Achilleid*, and the same notes in Book 1 of the *Thebaid* that Iris is the passage of the gods.
Fol. 158, line 4.

The two beams signifying Castor and Pollux were called among the Lacedaemonians Δίκαρα, as it seems to me Plutarch relates. And their figure we [?] shall place below, together with the character or cipher that the astrologers have introduced in the Zodiac for them, taken without doubt from the antique. Hence I give little credit, in this particular, to the thought of Joseph Scaliger, who in his *Annotations on Manilius* holds that this cipher derives from another figure.
qm: The word in the book (“we shall not place”) contradicts the continuation of the sentence; most likely a misprint; translated “shall place”.

blocks.text: Fol. 158, line 40.

And besides the apparition of these brothers to the Locrians, described by Justin and reported by Cartari, very notable among the Romans was that of the same Castors, which occurred (as Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Valerius Maximus, Plutarch and others write) at Lake Regillus, in the victory that Aulus Postumius the dictator won over the Latins. In token of which coins were afterwards struck, one of which has been represented in the principal figure.

The image of Liberty placed here below has been taken from the reverse of a medal of the Emperor Claudius. On it the open hand signifies those slaps on the cheek that were given to slaves in the very act of making them free, about which many have written; and singularly Cujas, in Book V of the *Observations*, at chapter 13. Nor did Sedulius mean anything else in Book V, where he describes the slaps given to CHRIST our Lord:

lines: For through these buffets our head is made curable;
these spittings, through our Lord, washed the figure;
with these slaps the greatest Liberty applauded us.
blocks.author: Sedulius

blocks.text: Fol. 160, line 27.

The passage in Gellius is in Book 7, at chapter 4, drawn from Caelius Sabinus, an ancient jurist, from whom it seems to me rather to draw the contrary; namely that some slaves were sold with the cap on the head, on whose account the seller would then have nothing at all to make good to the buyer; since the cap meant that everyone, in buying them, should look to his own affairs. For which reason the aediles at other times decreed that sellers of slaves should declare themselves in publishing their qualities, and in a sort of large schedule say whether they were fugitives, vagabonds or the like. And this is read in the same Gellius in Book 4, at chapter 2, and in my Commentary on Slaves at fol. 31. So that having the cap on the head (in my belief) meant: let him who gambles bear his own loss, and let the buyer take care.
Fol. 163, line 41.

Tommaso Filologo of Ravenna, an excellent physician in the age of our fathers, had this fable of Juno at heart; he had it marked on many of his medals; and in imitation of him one has been represented below. And the same invention of the principal fable is held, charmingly painted on a small picture, by Signor Andrea Spinola, son of the late Francesco, a Genoese gentleman, worthy of the love of all honourable men. And this poetic invention, as to the colouring of the lilies, is very like that which is read of the roses in Constantine Caesar, Book 11, chapter 18: that when Cupid was dancing in heaven he spilled with a wing a great cup of nectar, and that that liquor, dripping on the earth, coloured the roses, which they hold had previously been white. Others attribute it to the prick of a thorn in Venus's foot, as is read in the same.
Fol. 165, line 16.

This medal of the Emperor Nerva that is cited I have always held to be an empty fancy. And I am confirmed in my opinion all the more on seeing that Adolph Occo, a most diligent collector of antiquities of this kind, cites two medals of Nerva with this inscription “Fortune of the Roman People”, and says that on the first is seen a seated figure with a branch in the right hand, and in the left a plain spear. On the other medal he relates that the same figure holds in the right hand ears of corn and poppy, in the left a spear. It must therefore be that our Author has come upon a medal either worn or spoiled by cleaners, who, to the great prejudice of antiquity, form for us new letters and figures at their pleasure.
Fol. 168, last line.
Whoever wished to know how the knot of Hercules was made can derive it from these words of Macrobius in Book 1 of the *Saturnalia*, at chapter 19:

lines: That the Sun is worshipped in Mercury is clear also from the caduceus, which the Egyptians fashioned, to be consecrated to Mercury, in the form of serpents, male and female, joined together. These serpents are bound to each other in the middle part of their coil with a knot which they call the knot of Hercules; and their first parts, bent back into a circle, with mouths pressed together [?], join the circuit of the circle; and afterwards the tails are drawn back to the handle of the caduceus, which is adorned with wings growing from the same part of the handle.
blocks.author: Macrobius
qm: In the book a comma stands in the wrong place, and the word “eyes” by the sense should be “mouths”; translated “mouths”.

blocks.text: So whoever sees the caduceus of the ancients understands what the knot of Hercules is. I said “of the ancients” because our painters do not know how to draw it.
Fol. 169, line 18.

The goddess Partunda, I think, must be read Pertunda, on the authority of Arnobius in Book 4 *Against the Gentiles*. It is quite true that St Augustine in Book 6 of the *City of God*, at chapter 7, calls her Partunda; but I take it for an error of the copyists.

On the cameo of the principal figure Modesty has been represented, as she is seen on the ancient medals of many empresses. And this to show the flammeum, of which the Author speaks further above at fol. 172 and further below at fol. 183.

The cameo of the principal figure represents Attis, the beloved of Cybele, taken from an ancient gem. And in this the cap, or Phrygian mitre, is to be noted, exactly like that seen in the Vatican Virgil on the heads of the Trojans, on the medals of the Emperor Hadrian on the head of Phrygia, and on the head of the Ganymede that was Monsignor R. Grimani's, Patriarch of Aquileia. But of this we shall speak elsewhere more copiously.
Fol. 178, line 5.

This narrative is taken from Pausanias in Book 7. But where the Author reports that from the member of Agdistis the pomegranate was born, Pausanias writes otherwise, and holds that it was the almond tree. Of the pomegranate, however, Arnobius makes mention, who describes this whole fable with great diligence in Book 5 *Against the Gentiles*.
Fol. 179, line 21.

This washing of Cybele was so solemn that in the ancient calendars notable mention of it is seen, as in the Rustic one published by Fulvio Orsini, who explains this term, called “Washing”, very elegantly. The same is seen in another ancient calendar of the time of Constantine the Great, newly published by the Most Illustrious Signor JOHANN GEORG HERWART of Hohenburg, etc. And in this is read “Hilaria. Rest. Washing.” Of the Hilaria Vopiscus makes mention at the very beginning of the life of the Emperor Aurelian, whose words will be understood by whoever couples them with what Herodian writes in Book 1 of his *Histories*, and St Augustine in Book 2 of the *City of God*, at chapters 4 and 5. Not far from these goes Prudentius in his *Wreaths*, in Hymn X.

But Arnobius notes a fine point at the end of Book 7 *Against the Gentiles*: that Attalus sent to Rome nothing but a stone, not very large, black, and made like a barrel in relief, which was afterwards set in the statue of the Great Mother in place of a face. And this is what Prudentius meant in the place cited above, when he said through the mouth of St Romanus the Martyr that a black stone with a woman's face, set in silver, was carried round on a cart. And this was in the procession of the Idaean Mother, before which the senators ran on foot, barefoot. But since we have come to the subject of the earth, it will not be unbecoming to put here her image in that posture which among the ancients signified her firmness.

They called this one “Stable”, as is read on a medal of the Emperor Commodus, whereas on another, of Julia, wife of Septimius Severus, she is called Fecundity. And rightly, because the earth is supremely fecund, as the poets give her the epithet of all-bearing. On this medal see Sebastiano Erizzo.

The Temple of Vesta has been taken from a gold medal of the Emperor Titus, where two figures are seen with spears in their hands outside the temple, whom I would not dare to call Vestals. In the cameos the image of Vesta is seen, likewise taken from ancient medals. One of them holds in her hand the lamp to show the eternal fire (unless it is a capeduncula). The other holds the Palladium, which, as far as is seen in an ancient cameo recorded in this book at fol. 321, was an armed figure, of a posture like the Egyptian deities, as Apollodorus relates in Book 3 of the *Library*, and Procopius in Book 1 of the *Gothic War*. And about this temple I do not know how far to believe Landino, cited a little further down on the next page.

In the cameos Ceres has been depicted with torches, taken from ancient denarii: with the plough, and with the sow. Beneath her chariot is seen the most ancient symbol of Sicily, placed in many ancient monuments, on which see Antonio Agostini in the Third Dialogue, and the *Syracuse* of Don Vincenzo Mirabella in more than one place. As for the serpents that draw the chariot of Ceres, the modern painters sin intolerably, making them winged and four-footed, against the testimony of all ancient monuments. Yet the poets call them *Dracones*. That is true; but for all that they never meant anything other than the serpents of the figure that we have represented.

And that it is so, let Virgil be read in the matter of Laocoon, and let the statue of the same in the Belvedere be gone to see. The like is seen on the chariot of Triptolemus further down, at fol. 209, and in other places. I certainly remember having seen at other times a most ancient vase of agate, decorated on the outside with stories in low relief, in which likewise Ceres was seen, with the chariot drawn by serpents of this sort. And the same is seen on many medals where Aesculapius is represented, and in other such stories or fables of the ancients; as in the Dragon of the Hesperides, etc. And the serpents of the caduceus Macrobius calls *Dracones* in Book 1 of the *Saturnalia*, at chapter 19.

In the two upper cameos Triptolemus is represented. The first is taken from a well-worked carnelian; the second from a Greek medal of Antoninus Pius, which I have. In both the chariot is seen drawn by serpents. In the two lower cameos Liber and Libera are represented, that is Proserpina, of whom see Arnobius in Book V *Against the Gentiles*, who makes mention of the Sebadian mysteries, which were not, as the Author says at fol. 216, peoples of Egypt, but ceremonies of Jupiter Sebadius, or Savazius as some call him; see Mitalerius on Valerius Maximus.
Fol. 195, line 23.

To all this that has been said about the profanity (so to speak) of beans, let there be added the opinion of the ancient commentator on Juvenal, who at the end of Satire 15 writes that beans are born of human blood, and that their flowers are likewise changed into blood. See Acron on Horace, in Book 2, Satire 7, and Lactantius Placidus on the 4th book of Statius's *Thebaid*.
The principal image has been taken from an ancient intaglio, like the cameos too, in one of which Vertumnus is seen, in the other Pales.
Fol. 198, line 37.

Beside this goddess Pales, a female, there was a god Pales, a male, minister of Jupiter, and steward, as they say. So writes Caesius in Arnobius in Book 3 *Against the Gentiles*, and Martianus and Servius too make mention of Pales as a male.
Fol. 205, line 29.

What the Author says about the covered paintings is taken from Juvenal, who in Satire 6, from verse 312 to 343, most falsely touches on these gatherings of women, and the rascalities that were committed there in his time.
