Nor was this goddess so averse to wine as is here related; on the contrary she drank a full jar of it, for which reason she was very well beaten by her husband with rods of myrtle; as Sextus Clodius the grammarian relates in Arnobius in Book 5 *Against the Gentiles*, and he touches on it in passing in Book 1 too.
Fol. 206, line 1.

The author of the *Historia Miscella* writes that in the reign of Maurice, Menas, governor of Egypt, saw in the river Nile, in the place that was then called Delta, two animals of human form; and that one had the likeness of a male, the other of a female. The male had a large chest, a terrible face, red hair with some white among it, and was naked down to the loins; and the rest stayed under water. The female had breasts, and the face of a woman, and long hair. They remained on the surface of the water a long time, gazed at and gazed at again by the people, who had gathered in great crowds at the spectacle. Then they plunged under the water and appeared no more. And of all this Menas gave an account to the emperor. The same is read in Cedrenus.

This spread of cloth is seen on almost all the ancient deities that had to do with water. And it can be noted in this book at fol. 239. And I remember having seen in Rome, in St Peter's under the Confession, an ancient marble sarcophagus, which once served for the ashes of Junius Bassus, prefect of Rome, where the Nile is seen from the belly upwards under the feet of Joseph the Patriarch. The said river supports with both arms a flying veil, which arches over his head, of which Virgil made marvellous use:

lines: And opposite, the Nile, grieving with his mighty body,
spreading out his folds and with his whole garment calling
the conquered into his azure lap and hidden streams.
blocks.author: Virgil

blocks.text: On the Sirens see A. Agostini in the *Dialogues*, and F. Orsini in the *Roman Families*: in the Petronia and in the Valeria. But as to this last I incline strongly to the opinion of Gio. Vivianus, reported by Livinus Torrentius [?] on Suetonius, in the life of the Emperor Claudius at chapter 13: that it is not a Siren but Jupiter Carius. And as to the cognomen Aciscolus, I hold neither with Orsini nor with Vivianus, seeing that *Aciscolus*, as is read in the ancient glossaries, is the mason's hammer, and *Aciscolarius* in the same is the stonecutter, or stone-chiseller, as we choose to call him. Read Hadrianus Turnebus in Book 27, chapter 10, and in Book 28, chapter 5. Besides, on the medal itself there is likewise seen a hammer or axe, similar to that which is found in many ancient inscriptions, a sign that that monument had nothing to do with that chapter of the 12 Tables:
qm: There is a misprint in the name in the book: “Lenino” is printed, whereas the correct form is “Livinus” (the scholar Livinus Torrentius); the name is corrected to “Livinus Torrentius”.

lines: Do not smooth the pyre with an axe.
blocks.author: Twelve Tables

blocks.text: The principal image has been taken from an ancient half-relief found in a sarcophagus in my time in Rome, of which, and of other things, a short account that I then made of it will be read here below. The cameo has been taken from an intaglio in carnelian of most beautiful colour, which was at other times in the hands of Monsignor de PEIRESC, Royal Senator in the court of Parliament of Aix in Provence, a gentleman most knowledgeable in all these matters.

In the year 1608, in the month of February, while a vineyard of the Signori Leni outside the gate called St Sebastian's, near Capo di Bove, was being worked, besides many other vestiges of antiquity, such as of a temple of Minerva and Rhamnusia built, as is believed, by Herodes Atticus, a noble sophist of the time of Hadrian, besides some statues and heads of emperors, herms of illustrious men, and precious columns, there was uncovered an ancient sarcophagus, covered, of plain work but well conceived, and without any memorial of any sort. There was found in it a cloth, well preserved, of the finest wool, and a silk garment, both of that colour which the dry leaf shows, and they tended to rust-coloured, as the Latins say, with certain broad stripes in the woollen cloth which were of purple colour; and both these garments smelled strongly [?] of an odour that savoured of aromatics.
qm: There is a misprint in the book: a word close to “adored” is printed, whereas by the sense it should be “smelled”; translated “smelled”.

blocks.text: In the sarcophagus there was water, which through damp or rain had perhaps seeped in there. Besides the said garments there was a bulla of copper that had once been gilded, on which in half-relief is seen a soft young woman, who stands in a circle of waves, clothed over the flesh in a thin shift, and who ends from the waist downward in heads [?] of sea dogs and other animals which issue from her flanks and thighs, which she bears carved like a Siren. She raises, moreover, her right hand and arm in the act of striking, and with the left hand grips the neck of a sea horse as if she wished to strike it. There were besides in the sarcophagus two gold rings of great weight. In one, of uniform thickness, narrower than what could enter the base of a finger, was set a flat emerald, not cut, very beautiful; in the other, of more modern make, a green jasper with a boy carved on it, who, seated, gathers flowers.
qm: There is a misprint in the book: Cepi is printed, whereas by the sense it should be Capi (“heads”); translated “heads”.

blocks.text: And because the desire to know whose the said adornments were has made some people say strange things, I have determined to make trial, if I can, of reasoning about them with some verisimilitude; reckoning that it is not unbecoming in a person who loves these studies to go investigating those particulars which antiquity and time have sought to withdraw from our eyes and from our knowledge. Now it is to be known that this sarcophagus, or sepulchre, was upon the Appian Way, which kept the name of Appius Claudius the Censor, who had it paved across Italy as far as Brindisi.

Furthermore, the ancients were accustomed to build their sepulchres upon the roads, so that, as Varro says, they might in that way admonish passers-by that they too had to die. And it is very well known that in cities it was not lawful to bury, which was the custom not only among the Romans but among the Hebrews also, as is gathered from the sepulchre of Lazarus in St John, and from the widow's son raised in St Luke. For this purpose they chose for the most part the roads, as I have said, and Pliny the Younger proves it, who, speaking of the sepulchre of Pallas, freedman of the Emperor Claudius, says thus:

lines: There is the Tiburtine road; within the first milestone (I noted it recently) is the monument of Pallas, inscribed thus: “TO HIM THE SENATE, FOR HIS LOYALTY”, etc.
blocks.author: Pliny the Younger

blocks.text: And for this reason many cemeteries of the Christians lay beside the Salarian, Ardeatine, and Ostian roads, and others. At Capo di Bove, on the testimony of Cicero in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, it is a clear thing that many noble families had their sepulchres. He writes:

lines: Or do you, when you have gone out of the Porta Capena and see the sepulchres of the Calatini, the Scipios, the Servilii, the Metelli, think them wretched?
blocks.author: Cicero

blocks.text: So that one must almost conclude that the present one, of which we are treating, is one of those named, and this can be proved without difficulty, so far as antiquity and the injury done by him who left the chest bare and carried off the rest allow.

lines: Since fates have been given to the sepulchres themselves also.
blocks.author: Juvenal

blocks.text: And truly the diggers attest that around this sarcophagus solid buttresses of peperino have been found, which argue a notable building. But whose do we wish it to be? I for my part, if it is permitted me to guess, incline to Attilius Calatinus, who in the year 496 from the foundation of the City, as stands in the Fasti, and 254 before the Nativity of Christ, triumphed “from Sicily over the Carthaginians” (EX SICILIA DE POENEIS), a man of great valour, as is read in Florus and Cornelius Nepos. And although there is not seen on the sarcophagus what in the time of Cicero was read on the sepulchre:

lines: Very many nations and peoples agree with one voice that he was a foremost man.
blocks.author: Cicero

blocks.text: we have already said that the ornaments of the sepulchre have gone, which has happened to so many others that are seen along this road left despoiled. The reasons of my conjecture are the aforesaid appearance of a large and magnificent sepulchre, the fragments of an equestrian statue seen by me, and the cloth, which I judge to have been a chlamys, very rich and abundant in material. Certain people, however, have judged that there were many garments. I believe not, since the statues show us that a man wore about him a cloth so great that the warehouses now would not hold it at all. For no other reason, I think, did Juvenal call the toga *Auloca* [?], or, as we should say, arras hangings.
qm: The word is apparently a corrupted Latin “hangings”; left as printed.

blocks.text: The colour of the said cloth I do not doubt was purple at the edge, since the mark of it is still seen. Nor was the purple of one colour only, as some imagine. For Vitruvius writes that there were found some drawn toward black, some red, and some violet, which differences he ascribes to the different positions of the world where the shellfish were fished. This one of ours will be of the dark, of the colour of porphyry, which has likewise got from purple the name of Porphyrite. The odour is that very one which is perceived in the corpses that come to us from Egypt, called by an Arabic name mummies, and it is of myrrh, if the sense of smell does not deceive us.

The copper bulla served as the cover of the fibula, with which the chlamys was buckled over the left shoulder, and an example of it is seen on the Capitol, in the Court of the Conservators, in a cuirassed statue of Constantine, and in the house of the same Conservators in a head with the bust of Julius Caesar; or, as they more frequently did, over the right shoulder. Isidore says:

lines: A chlamys is that which is put on from one side and is not sewn, but is fastened with a fibula.
blocks.author: Isidore

blocks.text: And this fibula was either turned plain in the cover, or made of some gem, or else had some figure, as on a marble head with the bust of the Emperor Hadrian I have myself seen on the cover of the fibula the portraits of Hadrian and Sabina, husband and wife, well made in low relief. On the present one Scylla, symbol of Sicily, with which Calatinus had to do, is delicately carved. And it seems that the master (though more ancient) had before his eyes those verses of Virgil in Eclogue 6, repeated a little differently in the *Ciris*:

lines: Why should I speak of Scylla, daughter of Nisus, or of her whom rumour has followed,
white, her loins girt about with barking monsters,
to have harried the Dulichian ships, and in the deep gulf,
ah, to have torn timid sailors with sea dogs?
blocks.author: Virgil

blocks.text: And those others of Silius Italicus, from which it is gathered that she was borne as a device in war upon the helmet also:

lines: The man had a helmet of defence, on whose crown there rose
a triple crest, streaming a mane of Suebian hair.
Above it Scylla, hurling the weight of a broken oar,
leaned over and spread wide the savage jaws of dogs.
blocks.author: Silius Italicus

blocks.text: Dalechamp notes on Athenaeus that the Magi of Persia kindled fire on the mountains, and with certain little bundles of vervain in their hands sang certain verses of theirs and prophesied. And I remember reading in Maximus of Tyre that in Persia, when adding wood to the sacred fire, they were accustomed to say, “Eat, Lord Fire.” Let him not laugh who can. So it will be no wonder if Calatinus wore her as an ornament of the chlamys, or paludamentum, as we choose to call it. The rings also breathe much antiquity; and first, the one that holds the emerald, being narrow in the bore, has given some people cause to think that it might be a woman's or a child's. But they have not noticed in Pliny what he writes, that in his time they were accustomed to wear rings on all the fingers and at all the joints.

lines: This one alone (he speaks of the infamous finger) is now excepted; all the others are weighed down, and even the joints severally with other, smaller ones.
blocks.author: Pliny

blocks.text: And it will be no wonder that Attilius Calatinus, much earlier, as an excellent man, used some singularity, since Duilius also, who conquered the Carthaginians at sea, a contemporary of Calatinus, as Cicero writes:

lines: He was frequently delighted with a torch and a flute-player, which as a private man he had taken for himself without any precedent.
blocks.author: Cicero

blocks.text: The emerald is not cut, because, as the same Pliny writes, the masters who cut gems of this kind make use of it to refresh the sight. Therefore, he writes:

lines: By decree of men they are spared, being forbidden to be engraved.
blocks.author: Pliny

blocks.text: Nor is it a wonder that the rings are of such weight, since the same Author elsewhere, speaking likewise of rings, says:

lines: Others now display their weight.
blocks.author: Pliny

blocks.text: In contrast to Crispinus, who, effeminate, as Juvenal writes, found for his delights summer rings thin and light. And let this much suffice, for a man occupied with other things, on this particular. And if the narration is more conjectural than definitive, let the blame be given to long age, which “corrupts not a few things and takes away many”, so as to triumph not only over men but over their names also.
Fol. 210, last line.

The figure of Palaemon is seen on the medals of Corinth, on a cameo of the Patriarch Grimani, and on an ancient intaglio in the *Dactyliotheca* of Abraham Gorlaeus. From all these things the figure written below has been formed.

In the uppermost cameo Neptune is seen with the dolphin in his hand: because (as Eratosthenes writes in Hyginus) Neptune, wishing to take Amphitrite for wife, and she wishing to live in virginity, she fled to Atlas, to stay hidden there. Now Neptune sent many to seek her, and among these one called by name Dolphin, who after much wandering found her at last, and persuaded her to be content to take Neptune for husband. And hence it comes (says Eratosthenes) that the sculptors, in making Neptune, put a dolphin in his hand or under his foot.

The Canopus drawn in the cameo is a figure by now so well known that it is not necessary to say anything more of it. And it is seen on so many medals, gems, and marbles that it is a marvel. The fire placed higher up has been taken from an ancient medal of a King of Persia who has Persian letters around his head. And this has been put there on the occasion of what the Author writes, further above at fol. 227. And it was the custom of the kings of these peoples to carry about with them in their armies the sacred fire as well, as is read in Evagrius in Book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, at chapter 14; and to have particular places for worshipping it, as Socrates writes in Book 7, at chapter 8, and Giovanni Zonaras in the 3rd volume of the *Annals*.
Fol. 215, line 22.
The medal of Vespasian with Neptune has no whip, but an acrostolium, or prow of a ship, as can be seen in Enea Vico, in the 3rd Table of the silver medals of Vespasian, number 28.
Fol. 216, line 34.
The image of Oceanus is seen in Rome, as here below, described and explained by Stephanus Pighius in his *Hercules Prodicius*.

Pighius holds that this image contains great mysteries, and whoever wishes to see them, let him read them in him, for he certainly says fine things. It will suffice me to touch briefly on certain principal points reported by the same for the explanation of the features of body and of the garb that he has about him. He has on his head (says he) a thin veil, to show that Heaven is clothed and bandaged by the clouds that issue from the sea, and that hence the fecundity in the earth is born for the benefit of plants and of every sort of herbs, so that the hair, beard, and body hair of this statue ingeniously resemble acanthus and other soft and pliant herbs.

He is handsome and comely of face, and from his forehead there sprouted two little horns, both to show the roar of the sea stirred up by the winds, and to give to understand that its motion, which we call flux and reflux, is derived from the Moon, who is called by Orpheus bull-horned (*tauricorne*). Let it be added that he is the origin of the springs and rivers, which antiquity, as has been said, likewise feigned with horns. He has in his left hand an oar, or rudder, whichever it be, to show that with this instrument men have taken courage to venture far into him; he leans on a sea monster, as being the begetter of great and prodigious beasts. So far Pighius, in brief.
Fol. 218, line 13.

This Derceto was the same as Dagon, of whom mention is made in Sacred Scripture, as in the 1st Book of Kings, at chapter 5, and in the 1st of Maccabees, at chapter 10; and see Antonio of Lebrissa in his *Quinquagena*, at chapter 6. The image of Dagon, or Derceto [?], is seen at fol. 1 of this book, on the head of the statue of Semiramis.
qm: There is a misprint in the name in the book: Decreto is printed, whereas elsewhere in the same book it is Derceto; translated with the correct name “Derceto”.

blocks.text: In the principal figure, in the cameos, the rivers Hiberus, Bragada, and Danube have been represented, taken from the medals.
Fol. 222, line 27.

This custom of cutting off the hair and offering it to the rivers is touched on by Philostratus in Book 4 of the life of Apollonius of Tyana; by the same in the *Heroes*, in Ajax Telamonius. They offered it also to other deities, as is seen in Dio Chrysostom, in oration 35; in Diphilus in Athenaeus, in Book 6; in Censorinus; in Statius in several places; in Ammianus Marcellinus in Book 22.

In the figure of the Nile the draughtsman has taken the licence of not putting in all the children who were to go there. And they ought to have been 16. Let Stephanus Pighius be read in his *Hercules Prodicius*; Philostratus in the first book of the *Imagines*; Lucian in the *Precepts for Rhetoricians*. The festivals that were held in Egypt in honour of this river are touched on by St Gregory Nazianzen in the 2nd oration against Julian the Apostate; by Nonnus, scholiast of the same; by Heliodorus in the 9th book of the *Ethiopian Matters*. See our exposition of the Table of Isis.

Aristides writes a marvellous particular about the water of this river: that, carried far, it does not spoil; that in Egypt it is kept for three, four, and more years, and that it takes praise from old age, as wine does with us. Athenaeus adds that Ptolemy Philadelphus used to send some of this water into Syria to Berenice his daughter, married to King Antiochus, so that it might serve her for drinking. And it is not incredible, since Seneca writes that there is no river that has water of a sweeter taste, and Spartianus confirms it in the life of Pescennius Niger.

Plutarch writes in the short work *On Isis and Osiris* that the water of this river fattens whoever drinks it; and this saying was confirmed to me by the living practice of a person of great authority, who was some time in Egypt and experienced this particular in himself.
The principal image and the cameo have been taken from ancient intaglios.
Fol. 219, at the end.

Here by necessity the Nymphs had to stand, deities of rivers, fountains, and lakes, so renowned in the poets, in Claudian and in Martial in particular. Their images are seen in an ancient marble in Rome, in which is read the name of a certain Priscilla.

And a similar sculpture I once saw in Rome in the house of the Vittorii, where stood the name of one Epictetus, a slave water-carrier of an Emperor. And hence come the nymphaea, places assigned to waters, which are read of in Publius Victor and in some other place, although Zonaras assigns them to another use. And in the design set above it seems to me that the sculptor has made marvellous use of the rule of Vitruvius, in Book 1, at chapter 2, namely that to Venus, to Flora, to Proserpina, and to the Nymphs one should build in the Corinthian order, because of the slenderness, and the gracility, so to speak, that is seen in their bodies.
Fol. 246, line 32.
Dio is not the historian, but the philosopher, in the fifth Oration, which he entitles *Libyan Fable*.

The Sphinx and the Chimera have been taken from ancient monuments, and the two cameos are likewise from ancient intaglios. In one is Oedipus before the Sphinx, who sits on the Phycean rock, as Apollodorus calls it; in the other Bellerophon, who fights with the Chimera, and this last is seen very frequently on the coins of Corinth. On the Lamiae see Delrio in the *Magical Disquisitions*.
Fol. 248, line 34.
Pliny does not say that the Sphinx was a savage numen. His words are these:

lines: Before these is a Sphinx, even more to be wondered at [?]; where wild are the places of those dwelling nearby [?].
blocks.author: Pliny
qm: The Latin quotation is corrupt at this place and breaks off; translated literally as far as the text allows.
The Latin quotation breaks off at this place as well; translated literally as far as the text allows.

blocks.text: which Landino translates thus:

lines: Before these is a Sphinx, all the more marvellous because it is in wild places.
blocks.author: Landino

blocks.text: And well.
Fol. 251, line 30.

The ancients held Fate in veneration under three images of women, represented as here below. And they have been taken from an ancient gold medal of the Emperor Diocletian, seen by me at other times in Rome, with this inscription: “TO THE VICTORIOUS FATES”. It is quite true that, according to the understanding of Procopius, these will be the Parcae. For he writes in Book 1 of the Goths [?] that the temple of Janus was in the Forum, before the Curia, not far from the three Fates, for in that manner the Romans call the Parcae. And Apuleius is of this opinion also in his book *On the World*. And from this take their origin the fairies of the common people, and of our writers of romances. See Father Delrio.
qm: In the book a word, “war”, is apparently omitted — “in Book 1 of the war with the Goths”; translated according to the sense.

blocks.text: The cameos have been taken from carnelians and other ancient gems. On one is seen Mercury, who draws a soul out of Hell with his rod, as the poets sing. On another Mercury and Philology, or the like.
The images of Peace that are seen in the ovals are taken from medals. And of the one that is winged Gio. Vivianus discourses gracefully, in Adolph Occo, on the medals of the Emperor Claudius.
Fol. 222, line 17.

This noteworthy point of the Author's is clearly seen in the statue of the Emperor M. Aurelius, in Rome on the Capitol, from which, however, the Moderns have strayed. The like is seen on the medals of the Emperor Probus and Constantine, and of others, in the allocutions of other Emperors, and in other ancient monuments.

In the two cameos there have been represented, in one Mercury, who bridles Pegasus, and in the other the same running with a wreath in his hand, symbol of some victory obtained in the race. The first has been taken from a medal of Antinous in Sebastiano Erizzo, and a similar figure was to be seen in one of the cameos of Monsignor the Patriarch Grimani, of glorious memory, which may be Mercury as much as Bellerophon. The second has been taken from an ancient intaglio.

In the figures of the cameos are seen the herms, or square statues of Mercury, taken from two ancient intaglios. And a similar thing is seen on a Roman denarius of the Titia family, on which see F. Orsini under the same family. And of herms in particular I once saw a fine little Commentary written by Achilles Statius, printed in Rome, with the figures, which were many, taken from many [?] ancient statues of this sort. Similar to the herms was, in my opinion, the god Terminus, whose image is seen on a silver medal of Augustus, as here below.
qm: One letter in this word cannot be read on the scan; by the sense it is “many”.

blocks.text: And that among the termini, which were of many sorts, this figure was included also, is gathered from Hyginus, who in the collection of the authors that treat of rural matters records a terminus of this sort, called by him *Hermula*. Of Terminus Lactantius reasons in Book 1, at chapter 20, from whose words can be drawn the explanation of an enigma which Varro composed on this deity. With the terminus the ancients were accustomed to bury ashes, charcoals, fragments of baked clay, broken glass, bones somewhat burnt, lime, gypsum, and the like, as a sign, as Siculus Flaccus says, of a boundary set in that place.

And on the subject of charcoals, the same is noted also by St Augustine in Book 21 of the *City of God*, at chapter 4, as the Most Illustrious Signor MARCUS WELSER observes in Book 4 of his most learned *History of Augusta*, a most accomplished gentleman, who has passed to a better life, with extreme grief of the learned, while I was writing these things, on the 24th of June. I add that Pliny relates in Book 35, at chapter 6, that some painters were accustomed to draw charcoals from sepulchres to make black colour of them. And in 1600 I remember having seen certain ancient vessels of baked clay found in the Guasto (as they call it) in our city, in which there were burnt bones and charcoals mixed with earth, which exceeded a thousand years and more of antiquity, as was conjectured from two medals of Augustus found inside them.

In foundations also charcoals are of great durability; and for that reason Vitruvius exhorts the use of them in Book 3, at chapter 3, and in Book 5, at chapter 12. And of the temple of Diana at Ephesus Hesychius writes it in particular, who says that it was a recommendation of Theodorus of Samos. And among us, in laying the foundations of the most noble Church of St Justina, to overcome the difficulties of the marshy ground, full of spring waters, recourse was had to piles, hurdles, sacks of wool, and charcoals, as D. Giacomo Cavacio writes in Book 6 of the history of St Justina under the year 1502.
Fol. 273, line 13.
Of this custom of throwing stones around the statues of Mercury, Scripture makes mention, in Proverbs, at chapter 26; and on this usage Alciato has formed a fine emblem.

This figure has been taken just as it stands, entire, from a book of Signor JOHANN GEORG HERWART, a most learned and most knowledgeable Councillor of His Most Serene Highness the Signor Duke of Bavaria. And it is found on an ancient marble that bears an inscription, from which it is seen that whatever is seen carved on it was dedicated to the gods of Egypt who share the same throne. And they will be Apis, Anubis, Serapis, and Ammon, who on the same marble are called brother gods.
Fol. 284, line 33.

This thought of the French concerning Hercules is marvellously expressed on a bas-relief of metal which is seen in my possession, and is such as follows. Here Hercules is seen in a garb almost that of Mercury. The caduceus and the wings at the feet are understood. The palm is a sign of victorious eloquence, for which reason in antiquity palms were fastened to the doors of the houses of advocates, as is read in Lucan and Juvenal. The base, or little pillar, on which he leans, signifies the steadiness of eloquence. The fire that issues from the vase, its impetuosity. The star and the moon, its clearness and nobility.

Not very far from this thought is the Hercules Musagetes, or, as we should say, leader of the Muses, expressed by the ancients in the manner that will be shown here below: to give us to understand, as the rhetorician Eumenius writes, that the quiet of the Muses has need of the defence of Hercules, and the valour of Hercules of the voice and song of those. So Eumenius, to serve his purpose, who makes use also of the example of Fulvius, who in the circus built the temple common to Hercules and the Muses. But it must be that antiquity regulated itself by another thought, since it gave into the hands of Hercules the cithara and the plectrum, as is seen in a most beautiful cameo of the late Patriarch of Aquileia, and on the medals of the Pomponia family, of which the extract is here below.
Fol. 225, line 33.
Hercules on the medals of the Emperors Diocletian and Maximian is seen armed with almost all arms, having moreover a trophy in his hand.

In two cameos are seen two of the principal labours of Hercules. One as it is seen on the medals, of the dragon of the Hesperides, which is likewise without wings and without feet, as we have said elsewhere in these Annotations. The other of Cerberus tamed, as was to be seen in an ancient cameo in the possession of Monsignor Grimani, Patriarch of Aquileia. The club, or mace, of Hercules has likewise been taken from the monuments of antiquity, for any other form is false.

figs.pt: Два Геркулеса — с луком и с трофеем

blocks.text: Fol. 289, last line.

The Hercules here touched on is seen expressed in Rome, on the Capitol, in the Palace of the Conservators, in a most beautiful bronze statue. They represent him young, and without a beard. And of that age few are seen.
With Hercules the god Semo Sancus of the Sabines was of the same features, as is read in Festus Pompeius and Varro. And of this the figure is seen on the ancient denarii, as below.

Whoever wishes more of it, let him read F. Orsini in the *Families*, and Pedro Chacón in a little Treatise of his on this, printed in Rome with other works of his, in the year 1608, from which Cardinal Baronio dissents in the *Annals*, in the first volume.
Fol. 291, line 36.

I have observed in ancient monuments that quite often where the tripod stands, the griffin also stands. Of this (whether beast or bird it may have been) see Antonio Agostini, and our Exposition of the Isiac Table. And it is certain that antiquity held it to be a solar animal. But, to say something also of ecclesiastical antiquities, our forebears were accustomed to put griffins in the porches of the doors of churches, as that usage is seen preserved even today before our Cathedral, and at the door of the most noble Church of St Justina, where in the one place and the other lions also are seen.

And as to the griffin, I would say that the ancients believed that it was the guardian of the gold mines, as is read in Pliny, and in the Ape of Pliny, Solinus, if I am not mistaken. The poets formed the same conception of it, so that Claudian, writing to Serena, daughter of Theodosius, says that at the wedding of Orpheus, among various animals that honoured him with presents, the griffins brought with them a quantity of gold drawn from the mines of the Hyperborean mountains. Perhaps from here the modern alchemists drew the presidency of the Sun over gold; and see the Author at fol. 322.

Now among our people Faith was likened to gold, so that the Church sings of the martyrs that they were tried like gold in the furnace; and for this reason St Peter and St Paul in their Epistles made use more than once of this simile. So that, the Church being the mine of this gold, since there are contained in it the sacraments, which are compendia of our faith, with reason griffins are seen at its doors.

On an ancient carnelian (to return to profane matters) I have seen an Apollo clothed in a long garment with the quiver at his side, in the garb of Apollo Actius in the rest, who stands before an arula, or little altar, on which a griffin is seen.

Minerva in the principal figure, embraced with Mercury, has been taken from an ancient gem. Above, in the cameos, is seen a Hermathena taken from the medal of the Emperor Hadrian cited by Aldus Manutius in the exposition of the Epistles written to Atticus by Cicero; the Hermeracles, likewise cited by Cicero, has been taken from Pighius; although this too might be Hercules and Mercury, entire, embraced together, as was seen of Mercury and of Minerva. This last, armed, was represented as below.

And the serpent coiled around the bow has been taken from a most beautiful and most ancient large carnelian, which was Antonio Baisio's, cut by the hand of Antiphilus, on the reverse of which it was read that Dracon, son of Theagenes, a valiant archer, dedicated it to Minerva. The two other cameos have been taken from a small medal of Domitian which I have by me, most beautiful and very well preserved, with some others of the same subject.

Antonio Agostini, a most singular man, says in his 5th Dialogue on the medals that the aegis was an armour of the neck and of the chest. Which is not absolutely true. And as to the neck, I hold no. As to the chest alone, neither is this true, since on a statue of Pallas of mine the aegis covers the back also. And a similar one was once in Rome, in the hands of a friend of mine. But very much to the purpose of this place are the words of Servius, on the eighth book of the *Aeneid*, at that verse:

lines: And the dread aegis, arms of angered Pallas,
blocks.author: Virgil, Aeneid, Book VIII

blocks.text: The aegis (says Servius) is properly a covering of the chest made of bronze, which has in the middle the head of the Gorgon. And this, if it covers the chest of some deity, is called aegis; if it covers the chest of a man, as we see in the ancient statues of the emperors, it is called a cuirass. And hence Martial took occasion to flatter the Emperor Domitian, at the beginning of Book VII:

lines: While this is free, Caesar [?], it can be called a cuirass;
when it has sat on the sacred breast, it will be the aegis.
blocks.author: Martial, Book VII
qm: In the book an extra “and” stands before “Caesar”; it is not in Martial's verse; translated without it.

blocks.text: And the Poet perhaps wished to hit, as they say, upon the humour of Domitian, who wished to be held (as is gathered from Philostratus) a son of Pallas.
In the cameo the war column is represented, taken from the medals, as Festus calls it. And of it, and of the ancient usage of beginning war, see Father Valtrinus.
Fol. 306, line 13.
The Author could have said that this was Hercules, as indeed it is; see Occo, who cites Giraldi.
Fol. 306, line 27.

This fable of Prodicus is touched on by Philostratus in the life of Apollonius of Tyana, by Silius Italicus, who transferred it to Scipio Africanus the elder, by Justin Martyr in the *Apology*, and by others besides.

The winged Harpocrates is not so well represented as was needed. For upon the left arm there ought to have been propped a cornucopia, which the engraver forgot; he is seen, however, without wings too, and with the cornucopia alone, as here:
Fol. 313, Book II.

This thought of the prudent and wise government of the world is seen expressed on a medal of the Emperor M. Aurelius the Philosopher, of which we have represented the likeness here below; unless, however, whoever had it struck intended to allude to the conceit of Seneca, of which the Author speaks at fol. 151. The same Minerva, on another medal, likewise of M. Aurelius, is seen commanding I know not what to him who builds the ship Argo; of which see Apollodorus in the *Library*, Vettius Bassus on the *Phenomena* of Germanicus Caesar, Hyginus in the *Poetic Astronomy*. And it will mean the providence and wise mind of the Emperor in the government of the empire. And that working of Argus about the prow of the ship will perhaps wish to show that piece of speaking plank, taken from the oaks of Dodona, which, as Apollodorus and Hyginus note, was fixed to the prow of the said ship.

This figure of Jupiter, who strikes the Giants with lightning, has been taken from an ancient votive offering of the Cornelia family. The cameos from ancient intaglios of the heretics of the school of Valentinus and of Basilides, as many of them are seen in my book of the exposition of the Isiac Table, and some in Abraham Gorlaeus. But that the Giants had feet of this sort, besides Suidas cited by the Author, is found also in the ancient commentator on Statius, in Ovid, in Apollodorus, and in Sidonius, who notes in particular the heads of the serpents fixed in their soles, or, to say it better, in place of soles, exactly as is seen on the prodigious amulets (so to speak) of the above-written heretics.

The cameos have been taken from ancient denarii. And in them is seen Vulcan, wreathed, with the cap on his head; moreover the tongs and the hammer, as the Latins called them, with the anvil, in the middle. Vulcan is seen here, and at fol. 321; on Vulcan see the Mythologists. I for my part believe that Tubalcain was the first Vulcan, and that the name of this one has its origin from that infallibly.

This union of Mars and Venus I once saw gracefully expressed on a large ancient nicolo, of which the figure will be here below. A similar thought is seen on a medal of Faustina, wife of M. Aurelius the Philosopher, with the inscription “To Venus the Victorious”. And it seems to me that these men aimed at the most graceful verses of Lucretius at the beginning of his first Book.
In the cameos are seen Mars Gradivus and Mars the Victor, as he is figured on the ancient medals. The principal figure has been placed as the ancients made it.
The image of Fury was thus drawn by Zucchero, a skilled painter of our times. And the cameo has been taken from the medals of Trajan, which are more commonly judged to represent a prisoner.
Fol. 327, line 25.

In Augusta, in the garden of the late Most Illustrious Signor MARCUS WELSER, there is seen a free-standing stone, carved with figures on three sides, with an inscription on the fourth. The figures are Mercury, Victory, and Mars naked, as below. The inscription is such:

lines: Aelius Mont [?] Haeder [?] for his own safety and for that of P. Hisp. [?] Canavilus, son, and of Aelia Montestina, wife, fulfilled his vow willingly and deservedly; given, dedicated, consecrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, in the second consulship of Geta and the second of Plautianus.
qm: This name (Mont) is printed in the book abbreviated, and it is not quite clear what it means; left as printed.
This name (Haeder) is printed unclearly; left as printed.
This abbreviation (P. Hisp.) is not quite clear; left as printed.

blocks.text: And on the authority of this inscription the above-said most learned gentleman said that it could be demonstrated that the subscription of more than twenty laws of the Code is erroneous. And by the figures of this stone the religion of the Germans is seen, who adored principally Mercury, then Mars and Hercules, as Tacitus writes in his book on the customs of the Germans [?]; although this third is not seen there.
qm: There is a misprint in the name of the people in the book: “Grimani” is printed, whereas it should be “Germans” — the reference is to Tacitus's book on Germany; translated “Germans”.

blocks.text: The military standards have been taken from the Sepulchre of M. Pompeius Asper, where are seen the eagle and the images named by the ancient writers on military matters, and by the moderns also, among whom see Henry Savile. In the cameo is figured the reverse of a medal of the Emperor Trajan, on which Victory holds under her feet the battering ram, the formidable engine of antiquity, in place of which our artillery has succeeded. And the said medal will perhaps have been struck for some victory obtained with the battering ram.
The whole has been taken from ancient intaglios on diverse gems. The pomegranate, showing concord and union, means that from the union of forces and of minds Victory must needs be born.

This pomp of Bacchus has been taken entire from an ancient cameo, in which are seen all the improprieties of this filthiest part of idolatry: the nudity, the torches, the cymbals, the pipes, the satyrs, the dance [?], and the pouring out into every sort of wickedness, as many of the ancient Fathers have written in particular.
qm: The word at this place is broken in the book by a line-break and does not form a clear word; translated according to the sense — “the dance”.

blocks.text: In the cameo Comus is seen in the manner in which he was once seen in a cameo of Monsignor the Patriarch Grimani, with a drinking vessel beside him, upon a little column.
Fol. 343, line 14.

Silenus is seen in various antiquities, but excellently on two sarcophagi placed below, as to the person of the said. With him are the cymbal, the ass, and the wind horns for playing. In the cameo, moreover, is seen the cantharus, of which Virgil sang:

lines: And a heavy cantharus hung by its worn handle.
blocks.author: Virgil

blocks.text: Of this mad company the Bacchantes were no small part, who are seen expressed in various places. We shall put one of them here below, taken from a most beautiful cut sardonyx, which was the Most Christian King's, under the keeping of Monsignor de Bagarris. In this carving are seen the desperate, life-spurning outrages [?] which they committed at their mad festivals, the herms that served for indecent use, a satyr with cymbals and with the ferula, etc.
qm: There is a misprint in the book: a word close to “waning” is printed, whereas by the sense it should be “outrages”; translated “outrages”. **Misprints without [?]** (sense and grammar are not affected;…

blocks.text: This whole pomp has been taken from an ancient jasper of Monsignor de Bagarris, antiquary of the Most Christian King, drawn and explained excellently by Casaubon in his first book on Satiric Poetry, at chapter 2. It is indeed true that in our present design the painter has omitted a mask under the feet of the first boy, who carries the leg of Bacchus on his shoulder, and a vessel of wine overturned between the feet of the Satyr. In the cameo Bacchus has been put, with the cornucopia and with the tiger, taken from an ancient intaglio.
Fol. 346, line 3.

A trace of this usage of drinking from vessels that had the form of horns is seen expressed here in Padua on the marble of the triclinium, which they call Patavine, in the house of the Rannusii, drawn by Pedro Chacón in his Commentary on the Triclinium, and by Girolamo Mercuriale in the *Gymnastics*. Moreover, let Pliny be read where he describes the lioness of Arcesilaus, Book 27. Fulvio Orsini, a man most knowledgeable in antiquities, always held that the effigy with horns that is seen on the medals of Lysimachus was of Alexander the Great. And so I hold too.

This is part of the Chorus of Ariadne, taken from an ancient marble sarcophagus, on which the ancient chariot of four wheels is marvellous, since ordinarily it is wont to be of two. Of four, however, I have seen it also in Verona on a small ancient marble in low relief, on the façade of the Church of St Proculus. In this one of ours there is seen moreover the umbrella, or conopeum, called shameful by Horace, when he describes the delicacy of Cleopatra and Mark Antony. And a similar umbrella is seen on the ancient medals of King Agrippa.
Typhon in the cameo has been taken from ancient intaglios; Osiris, from the Table of His Most Serene Highness of Mantua; the hippopotamus, from the medals.

The amulets, or fascina, that are seen in the principal figure are taken from the originals which I have by me. And a small one, of gold, which was for some baby in swaddling clothes, is kept by Signor LUIGI CORRADINO, a most knowledgeable gentleman of our city. See the exposition of the Isiac Table at fol. 16 and 17.

In the cameo a most ancient statuette of Apollo has been portrayed, which I have, in which great conformity is seen between Priapus and Apollo. And because Priapus was made of fig wood, as is seen in the next verses of Horace, let it be observed that this was not by chance, but on purpose, in commemoration of the rascality which Bacchus used to satisfy the pact that he had with Prosymnus. Let Arnobius be read in Book 5 *Against the Gentiles*, and the exposition of the Hieroglyphic Table at the place cited.

But here it comes in handy to say that in Naples, with Signor GIO. VICENZO della PORTA, there was once seen an ancient lead tablet, two feet and three palms long, high half the length, on which, in Greek characters of the kind they call majuscule, there were read words of this sense: In the woods one lives a life without cares, far from ambition. In the woods liberty is acquired, and rest is found. In the middle of the said tablet was a little oval window, with its cover of bronze, which had on the outside the face of a Satyr; within, a wild vine that adorned it, with a small label in the middle, on which something of this sense was read: We love the woods and the caves.

In the void of the little window a tablet was seen, which had above a male member, and it had some at the feet of the tablet. On the border of the tablet was this word, “To the god”. Beside it were seen an ass, some stalks of reeds, the sickle, and a drinking vessel with two handles. He who has seen the drawing has said well that with reason they loved the woods and caves; for such knaveries in the open air could not fail to defile Heaven and the Sun, not to mention the eyes of anyone who had a tiny bit of honourable blush. And in this connection others have noted the priesthood of rustic Hercules, and the epithet of sylvan Hercules, who, if he was not Priapus, differed little from him.
The images of the Lares have been taken from a denarius of the Caesia family.

In the cameos are seen the Genius of the Roman people with a beard, and the same Roman people at the age of a youth, with a cornucopia behind the shoulders, though the engraver has made him anything else but that. At such an age he is seen on two fine little medals in my possession, one of which has for reverse a star, the other an extravagant building: with an inscription that perhaps wishes to allude to the festivals of the god Consus, which antiquity called Consualia. Nor is it a wonder that the Genius has been feigned with a beard, because the Genius of the Senate too is seen with a beard, on the medals of the Emperor Antoninus Pius, as below.

It is indeed true that on many Greek medals, as of Smyrna, of Tripolis, and of other cities, a beardless head is seen, which from the inscription is gathered to be of the Genius of the Senate, or the like. And in connection with a bearded Genius, I remember having seen in the hands of Signor EDMUND BRUTZ, an English gentleman, most curious about these things and a great friend of mine, a small tablet of marble, in half-relief, ancient, where the Genius was, as at a lectisternium, in the posture that is seen below:

The patera and the horn of plenty are the proper insignia of the Genius, and a thousand medals bear witness to it. The modius that he has on his head is also his, as will be shown further below. The serpent at the edge of the table is also a sign of the Genius, as Virgil noted too in the serpent seen coming out of the tomb of Anchises. The cakes on the rim of the table and the acerra in the hand of the woman who sits at his feet are signs of sacrifice.

The pig lower down, led by a boy, will be for a victim, because to the Genius this alone was fitting; and Theodorus Marcilius proves it, on the second Satire of Persius. Now the Genius with the cornucopia and with the patera is seen on the medals of Nero, of Titus, of Trajan, and of other emperors. On two medals, however, one of Constantine, the other of Maximinus, the Genius is seen, as below, with the modius on his head, as is seen also on another of Maximian Caesar struck in Carthage.

The medal of Maximinus is struck in Antioch, so that the Genius holds in his hand the head of the Sun, in accordance with the thought of Ausonius, who called Antioch the house of the laurel of Phoebus. And perhaps there is an allusion to the temple of Apollo Daphnaeus, on which see Ammianus Marcellinus. That of Constantine is struck in Alexandria, so that for this reason the Genius holds the head of Serapis in his hand. And see Ammianus in Book XXII. That cities, moreover, had a particular Genius is a known thing. Antioch pictured him in diverse ways. And here is his portrait, taken from the medals.

The principal image has been taken from an ancient little medal, on the reverse of which is an Apollo citharede with these words TO HOLY APOLLO. And it will be good, in this connection, to read Philostratus in the first book of the life of Apollonius. The 1st and 2nd cameos are of the same city. And this second has been taken from the ancient Itinerary Table, in which the nude figure at the feet of the seated one is of a river; for the engraver of ours has made it every other figure, not understanding the drawing. The 3rd is of Caesarea of Cappadocia, with the river Melas beneath the feet. The 4th likewise of Antioch, taken from a silver medal of Augustus.

And in the second the diadem is to be noted, as about the heads of our saints, on which see what I have said in explaining the Hieroglyphic Table, against the opinion of a learned man of our times, but too bold in such things. And because the aforesaid principal figure was not too well regulated, another has therefore been made.
Fol. 370, line 6.

The scourge in the hand of the Genius is a monstrous thing. Ordinarily he holds the cornucopia; and he is seen so made on thousands of medals. It is quite true that Bonus Eventus is seen with ears of corn and poppy, which the Author has perhaps taken for the scourge. And this one too is young, and nude, and has the patera in his hand.

figs.pt: Гений с рогом изобилия и патерой

blocks.text: The upper cameo has been taken from a medal of the Emperor Commodus, in which Fortuna Manens is figured thus, whom we should call stable and firm. And to this thought a passage of Horace tends, in Ode 29 of Book 3:

lines: Fortune, glad in her savage business, and
obstinate in playing her insolent game,
shifts uncertain honours about,
kind now to me, now to another. I praise her ABIDING.
blocks.author: Horace

blocks.text: And the person who had the medal struck perhaps wished to allude to some victory in the Circus games. The lower cameo is from a medal of Trajan; but a ship's prow has been omitted there, which is seen in the middle of the rudder that Fortune holds in her hand. And this will have been struck in memory of some good outcome by sea or river, having much conformity with Annona, or Abundance. For ordinarily the Fortuna of the land had a wheel added, as is seen on the medals where Fortuna Redux is represented. And see A. Agostini in the second Dialogue.

These figures are seen very frequently in the sepulchral memorials of the Greeks. And I for my part do not believe that he who had them made put into them so much mystery as the Author goes tracking out in them.

The Nemesis with wings has been taken from an ancient carnelian of mine, the other, without wings, from a Greek medal of Aurelius Caesar, on which it is read that the figure set above is the Nemesis of the people of Tyana. It is quite true that on the medal what she draws in front of her face is not a veil but rather I know not what, which is drawn out from the garment about the neck, in the manner in which, further above, at fol. 286, it is seen in the cameo of winged Peace. On high Justice is seen, as on the medals of Hadrian.

In the upper cameo there has been represented the intaglio of an ancient gem, in which Abundance is seen joined with Justice, in a very graceful knot of figures. In the hand of Justice is this bundle of those rods that the lictors anciently carried before the magistrates, taken from an ancient sepulchre.
Fol. 383, line 15.
A thought little different from that of Apelles was had in our days by Federigo Zucchero, a skilled painter.

In the cameo Fortuna is seen stretched on a bed, who, according to the opinion of Erizzo, will be the golden Fortuna of the Chamber of the Emperors. I hold her for the secure and unchangeable Fortuna. And perhaps the golden Fortuna had another form. And Julius Capitolinus makes mention of her in the life of Antoninus Pius, at the end. See the Author at fol. 427.
Fol. 397, last line.

The god Kairos, or Cero, is gracefully described by Phaedrus, freedman of the Emperor Tiberius, in Book V of his fables, although the title says TIME; which in no way contradicts the essential nature of Occasion, since this is nothing other than opportuneness of time. And in what follows about Callistratus the sculptor, I suspect that the Author has been mistaken in some way. For Callistratus did indeed describe in words the god Cero, already made by Lysippus, but did not sculpt or form him himself.

Of the Scythians, moreover, Q. Curtius does not say that they had Fortune without feet, nor that she had among them wings about her hands; but he puts into the mouth of one of their ambassadors sent to Alexander words either similar or little dissimilar:

lines: Put a bridle on your felicity, for in this way you will rule it more happily. They say that Fortune is without feet, and has only hands and feathers; take note that when she holds out her hands, she does not for all that allow anyone to lay hands on her feathers, etc.
blocks.author: Quintus Curtius

blocks.text: The ambassador wished in this way to give Alexander to understand the slipperiness of Fortune.
Fol. 412, line 18.
This design was once printed in a rather large form, in imitation of which the small one has been made that we give here. And some hold it to be a design of Doni.
This whole image has been taken from an ancient intaglio.
Fol. 397, line 35.

That the things recounted are modern inventions I hold not to be so; for besides my having an ancient carnelian in which Fortune is seen at sea, with the sail, just as our painters paint her, Signor LUIGI CORRADINO, a man of exquisite understanding about these things, has an ancient intaglio in carnelian by an excellent master, of which this is the figure.

Here are seen the waves and the sail, and moreover a swan that carries Fortune as if on its wings; a bird of very prosperous augury, so that it is said to Aeneas in Virgil at the beginning of the Aeneid:

lines: Behold twice six swans rejoicing in a column,
whom the bird of Jove, gliding from the region of the aether, was harrying in the open sky:
now in a long line they seem either to be settling on the earth
or already to be looking down upon the earth they have taken.
As they return, they sport with whirring wings. Etc.
blocks.author: Virgil

blocks.text: On this passage see Servius.
Fol. 404, line 8.
The Heavenly Cupid is seen in a most beautiful painting in the gallery of Signor LUIGI CORRADINO, from the design of the late Signor PAOLO AICARDO, a most learned and most courteous gentleman.
And the cameo has been taken from an ancient intaglio.

In the cameos Eros and Anteros are seen represented: either beneath the chariot of their mother, or wrestling together. On these see Enea Vico in the *Medals of Julius Caesar*, and Giraldi in Syntagma XIII. And let it be noted, in connection with Servius on Book 4 of the Aeneid, cited by Giraldi, that I have seen in more than one ancient intaglio Cupid in the act of tormenting and punishing him who does not love in return. And perhaps they were magic charms.

In the upper cameo the Cupid citharede has been taken from an ancient sardonyx given to me by Signor MARTINO SANDELLI, a man of exquisite letters and of the finest judgement, of whom I should say more if friendship did not forbid me. The lower ones are taken, one from the medal, the other from a gem.
Fol. 421, line 30.
This jest of Arcesilaus has in our days been gracefully expressed by Theodorus Gallo, a Flemish painter.
Fol. 423, line 30.

Ausonius's thought has been represented here below; and in a cameo the portrait of an ancient gem, which was in the study of Monsignor the Patriarch of Aquileia, in which two Amorini were seen binding to the cross that Lipsius calls decussate, and that we should call St Andrew's, Venus their mother.

In the cameo there has been represented the temple of Venus, as it stood in Paphos, a city of the island of Cyprus, taken from medals or ancient intaglios. And I have a small medal of the Empress Severina, on the reverse of which Venus holds in her hand this, which by others is called an apple, not very truly.
The principal figure, and the Amorino who plays with the swan, are from the antique. And the form of the scourge in the hand of Venus is to be noted, which has more of the fan than of anything else.
The cameo in which Cupid attends Venus his mother, who bathes, is an ancient work; but it ought to have been better made. And in such an act Venus is seen in a thousand antiquities.

The principal figure ought to be round, but the painter has made it oval for his own convenience. And this drawing of a gem is set down not only by Apian but also by Gio. Mario Mattio in Book 3 of the *Opinions*, and by Ramírez on Martial. The figure, moreover, that is entitled JOCUS I have seen expressed in some other ancient intaglio.
In the cameo is seen Venus Kallipyge, as she appears on the medals.
In the cameo stands the portrait of an ancient ring found once in the ruins of Spello; it is in Foligno in the hands of Signor NATALITIO BENEDETTI, an exquisite collector of ancient elegances.

In it is seen the most fortunate throw among the ancients of the game of knucklebones. This was the one that they called VENUS. And it was with four knucklebones, when all the faces of the knucklebone came up different, as is seen in the drawn gem. That this was the throw of Venus is inferred also from Cicero in the first book of *On Divination*, and from Martial in the *Apophoreta* at Epigram 14, with the title, IVORY KNUCKLEBONES.
THE END.
This figure was forgotten to be put in its place, therefore it must be put between numbers 52 and 53.
Addition to Cartari's Images, by Signor Lorenzo Pignoria.
Fol. 25, line 10.

Saturn had a sickle, as can be seen on the ancient denarii of the Memmian family, from which Ortelius took it, and on my coin of Caepio, and on the statue of Mithras that belonged to Orazio Mario Tigrino. Moreover, in Grotius's *Aratus* [?], printed by Raphelengius in the year 1600, on page 81 one sees the head of Saturn surrounded by a nimbus, with the harpe beside it, which resembles a sickle, as Grotius notes in the same book, at the figure of Perseus.
qm: “Aratro del Grotio”: the printed word is “Aratro” (“plough”); the sense requires “Arato” (Grotius's work on Aratus, *Syntagma Arateorum*, 1600). Rendered “Grotius's *Aratus* [?]”.

blocks.text: Fol. 39, line 12.

Janus was very often depicted by the ancients with two youthful faces, and so Ortelius has represented him. So too he stands on one ancient denarius, and on a piece of money of the sort that the ancients called *aes grave*; I have it. It is a thing of the sort that the common run of antiquaries call Weights, which they are not. For in antiquity weights were indeed made of copper, but in the form of balls, flattened, however, at the bottom to make them stand, and on top to mark on them either the mark of the weight or the name of the magistrate. But for the most part they were of stone, green or black, very hard.

Sebastiano Erizzo and Luca Peto record many of them. I have several, and on one, with letters formed of dots, one reads a Marcus Fusius; it is of exactly one ounce. Two others I have with the mark of the semuncia, and others larger. In later times, then, they were made of copper in square and round form, in various ways. And the collection of them made by Smetius and by Gruterus is worth seeing. The image of the young Janus is this one, unless it is, however, the Iana of Nigidius.
Fol. 110, line 27.

Cartari took this wreath of abrotano from Giraldi, in Syntagma XII, at fol. 369, who, however, says it on the opinion of others. I do not know of any ancient author who says so, but I defer to the truth. I know well that the female abrotano was a plant of the priests of Isis, and I say so in my Commentary on the Hieroglyphic Tablet of His Most Serene Highness of Mantua. And perhaps from here the error was born, if there is an error here at all.

Whoever wishes to see something concerning panic terror should read our notes on Emblem CXXII of Alciato, and the *Rhesus* of Euripides. In our own days a night in the year 1606 in the Paduan territory was notable for a terror more than Panic.

Signor Ottavio Rossi has recorded many fine particulars about the priest whom the Athenians called Bouphonos, in his *Brescian Memoirs*, at fol. 187. And of this ceremony, which Cartari touches on here, Porphyry speaks at length in Book II of *On Abstinence from Eating Meat*, at fol. 40 of the Latin version.
Fol. 325, line 32.

In Lycophron I have not managed to find what the author says here. It is found, however, in Alessandro Sardi, who wrote *On the Customs and Rites of the Nations*, in Book 3, at chapter 6, and in Caelius Rhodiginus, in Book 8, at chapter 2. And of these Fire-bearers (Πυρφόροι), as they were anciently called, Herodotus makes mention in Book 8, at fol. 452 of the Wechelian edition, and the Suda, and Julius Pollux; from these authors it is gathered that they were inviolable, like trumpeters and drummers nowadays.
Fol. 406, line 2.

The passage of Pausanias cited by the author is in Book 4, where he relates that Pindar called her Pherepolis, that is, guardian of the cities. Perhaps for this reason, on a small metal statue a span in size, in the possession of Signor Pompeo Pasqualino in Rome, towers are seen on the head of Fortune.

It is a great wonder that Cartari made no mention at all of the goddess Themis, of whom Pausanias nevertheless made mention in several places. According to what Eusebius writes of her in Book 2 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, at chapter 4, she was the wife of Jupiter and the mother of Minerva. Diodorus Siculus also speaks of her in Book 5, at chapter 15. Arnobius relates in Book 5 that at her command Deucalion and Pyrrha took stones from Mount Agdus in Phrygia, to restore the human race. And so it is seen that she was a prophetic goddess, as Apollodorus relates in the 1st book of his *Library*, and Diodorus Siculus, and Ovid in the 1st book of the *Metamorphoses*.
Now if Themis (as Cornutus writes) was she of whom he speaks thus:

lines: under whose protection we conclude contracts, make agreements, and keep the pacts in good faith
blocks.author: Cornutus

blocks.text: Then she will be Equity, whom the first emperors on their coins depicted standing, with scales in her right hand and a spear in her left. Those who succeeded them afterwards gave her the cornucopia in place of the spear, wishing to imply that abundance was more fitting [?] to Equity than the spear, often a symbol of war.
qm: “contraceuole”: the word does not exist; probably a misprint for *confaceuole* (“fitting”). Rendered “more fitting [?]”.

blocks.text: But if Themis were Justice, as Budaeus holds in the *Annotations on the Pandects*, she was depicted seated, with a patera in her hand, resting on a spear. And so she is on the medals of Hadrian, of Antoninus Pius, of Alexander Severus. Stephanus Pighius has printed an elegant discourse on the goddess Themis.
Fol. 488, line 27.
This authority of Macrobius reported by Cartari has made me believe that the fragment placed below belongs to a statue of Proserpina, or Libera, if we would rather call her that;

I had the drawing of it from the late Signor Paolo Gualdo, who was the owner of the statue and was archpriest of our cathedral, my most loving patron “while the fates allowed.” And on the figured band that goes around her chest and over her shoulders a most elegant sonnet has been written by Monsignor Antonio Querenghi, a great splendour of our city. And the same band has been explained in Latin by my Signor Girolamo Aleandro in his *Heliaca*, with a singular apparatus of varied and copious erudition, being praised as such by the same Monsignor Querenghi in another sonnet.

And worthy of notice (inasmuch as on the band one sees Minerva, Diana and Hercules) is the account of Pausanias in his account of Arcadia, which is the eighth book: that in Megalopolis there were to be seen statues of Proserpina and of Ceres; and that before Proserpina stood two young girls, who carried on their heads a little basket each, full of flowers; and that they were called the daughters of Damophon, but that others held that they were Minerva and Diana, who in company with Proserpina gathered flowers; that before Ceres stood Hercules, a cubit in size; and that Onomacritus writes that this Hercules was one of the Idaean Dactyls.

Lions in that manner are fitting for Pluto more than for Cybele. It is known that Pluto was the god of the earth; and yet, as Signor Aleandro says, no one is found who gives them to Pluto, as far as it has been possible to observe. The serpents that draw the chariot of Ceres I remember having seen thus fashioned in relief on a very ancient vase of gemstone. And on an ancient medal that I have, they draw the chariot of Triptolemus, fashioned in this manner.
Fol. 191, line 22.

The image of Attis is seen on fol. 188 [?], taken from an ancient marble that is in Rome, and from a ring gem. However, since a very beautiful one was found in Flanders in past years, I wished to place it in this spot.
qm: “si vede 188”: after “si vede” the words “a car.” (“at fol.”) are missing; rendered “is seen on fol. 188 [?]”. The marginal note at this paragraph is “Fol. 191, line 22”.

blocks.text: And whoever wishes to see more of them can read about them sufficiently in a Commentary of ours printed in Paris and reprinted in Venice with the title *Mysteries of M. D. M. I. and of Attis*. And Signor de Peiresc, Royal Councillor at Aix in Provence, a most learned and most noble gentleman, has a similar one; but his is in a more agitated cast and with a rougher face. With the one from Flanders there was found a hand of the same material, that is, of bronze, which I have likewise explained in the booklet cited above.
Which has some resemblance to a hand placed on a spear of the god Tillinus, explained and set out by Signor Ottavio Rossi in his *Brescian Memoirs*, on pages 128, 129.
To Tillinus.

But since Signor Girolamo Aleandro has done me the favour of writing to me his opinion about the hand of Tornax, somewhat different from what I have written about it, I did not wish to withhold it from the scholars who have a taste for this learned knowledge. He writes thus:

lines: On the occasion of having considered the little work of Your Worship, full of most beautiful erudition, I shall not fail to tell you that the bronze hand could have been made by someone out of his devotion, who was initiated both in the mysteries of Cybele and of Isis and also of Bacchus, it seeming to me that the figures contained in it may pertain to all three. For there is no doubt that to Cybele pertain the pine cone, the flutes, and the cymbals; to Bacchus the sickle for the grape harvest, the phallus, which may likewise belong to Isis, from what was written of Osiris.

The thyrsus, which I believe to be what Your Worship calls “a sceptre marked with a pine cone,” because on ancient wall paintings I have observed that the thyrsi that the Bacchantes hold in their hands are of the same form. The cithara too, which is seen next to the vine-dresser's sickle, may belong to Bacchus. To Isis it is clear that the sistrum belongs, and perhaps also the half-moon and the whip that was depicted everywhere in the hand of Horus, and to this Horus the tortoise also belongs, since I consider most true the explanation given of it by our Sandelli, because in a book of drawings that belonged to Fulvio Orsini, which today is preserved in the Vatican Library, among the other drawings of statuettes of that same Horus Harpocrates, there are two at whose feet a dog and a tortoise are seen. The serpent, as is known to Your Worship, may regard both Bacchus and Isis, and perhaps also the mysteries of Attis, as you discuss.
blocks.author: Girolamo Aleandro

blocks.text: So far Signor Aleandro, very learnedly.

chapters.title: Second title page of the Second Part and the publisher's dedication

blocks.text: Title page

NEW SECOND EDITION
OF THE TRUE AND NEW
IMAGES
OF THE GODS
OF THE INDIANS.
Dedication

TO THE VERY ILLUSTRIOUS
my most respected Signor

SIGNOR
PIERO BUARNO [?].
qm: “Piero Buarno”: so in the source, as in the first dedication; no other spelling is found. Rendered “Piero Buarno” [?] (the form of the name is not confirmed).

blocks.text: The memory that I keep of the favours received from Your Worship over a long span of time is so fresh and alive in my mind that, if I had an opportunity at hand as ready for showing myself grateful to you as I know how to wish for one, I would dare to promise myself some lightening of that weight with which your courtesy has loaded me in good measure. Therefore, until some turn of favourable occasion brings me something of greater moment for my aspirations, I offer to Your Worship this treatise, which under the name of the part on the Images of the Gods comes to light from my printing house; and I do so also in keeping with the mind of its author, who holds your worth in singular esteem and has given me a sign that he would be glad if I resolved to do so.

I see it as small in bulk, but I do not esteem it small as regards the opinion that I have heard formed of it by the experts, who hold the author to be a man who has few equals in the knowledge of this kind of antiquity. May Your Worship for now accept my affection, and keep for me your good favour, which I value as much as you know. May Our Lord God grant you prosperity. From Padua, 1 November 1614.

Your Worship's
most humble servant
Pietro Paolo Tozzi.

chapters.title: The Second Part of the Images of the Indian Gods

blocks.text:
SECOND PART
OF THE IMAGES OF THE GODS
OF THE INDIANS.
*Addition to Cartari by Lorenzo Pignoria.*

Herodotus, a sensible writer and not such a liar as he is commonly held to be, says of Egypt that it has more marvellous things than any other country, and that in it, above any other part of the world, there are to be seen works that the pen of writers cannot reach. And truly this remark of Herodotus cannot be called a hyperbole, since the pages, both sacred and profane, are full of the greatness, the strength and the riches of that very great and most noble kingdom. Nor was the glory of its ancient kings small in conquests and in carrying victorious arms against peoples both neighbouring and very distant.

For we read of Sesostris that he subdued Ethiopia, Scythia, Thrace, the Colchians and a good part of Asia Minor, and of Amasis that he made the island of Cyprus tributary. In earlier times (as is gathered from Diodorus Siculus) Osiris travelled through the world, from the desert borders of India to the sources of the Ister and to the sight of the Ocean; and of another king Manetho writes that he subjected the Phoenicians, the Medes and the Assyrians to his crown. And of others on the same subject many other things are read.

Now, if with their dominion their religion too passed to the conquered peoples, it seems to me nonsense to doubt it. Herodotus relates that the people of Colchis received circumcision from the Egyptians in this way, and in the same way the people of Phoenicia and of Syria; which, although it may not be very true (since of the Hebrews in particular we know what we must believe), nevertheless has much that is reasonable, since it is the custom of the conquered to adapt themselves to the customs, usages and rites of the conquerors. And who knows whether the cult of Isis among the Suebi in Germany, noted also by Tacitus, did not have its origin from here? All the more so because the idol of her among those peoples, made in the shape of a frigate, showed some trace of the daring voyages of the bold sailors of Egypt.

The Egyptians did not leave in peace those peoples either which, discovered and subdued within the memory of our fathers by the most valiant Portuguese nation, are included under the general name of the East Indies; for Herodotus writes, again, that Sesostris conquered the peoples around the sea that we now call Red (with a fleet of large galleys, we should say), and that, penetrating still further, he found a sea full of shoals and consequently not navigable, so that he was forced to turn back.

The Ptolemies went further, encouraged perhaps by some discovery of the earlier kings; for Philadelphus, eager to learn and to see new things, as Strabo too calls him, sent a certain Dionysius to explore the Indies, and he afterwards wrote books and reports about them. And Cornelius Nepos relates that a certain Eudoxus, fleeing from King Lathyrus, set out from the Arabian Gulf, today the Sea of Mecca or Red Sea, and wandered so long that he arrived at Cadiz: an undertaking that shows commerce and knowledge of the country.

And perhaps this Eudoxus is the same who in the time of Ptolemy Euergetes sailed to India and to many other places then unknown, as Strabo relates on the testimony of Heraclides Ponticus, though he laughs at it, for certain arguments of his that are not very solid, to tell the truth. But it was a universal heresy of the ancient geographers to hold as fables all the accounts of the new world. And they transmitted this vain opinion to men's minds with such force that even our grandfathers laughed at Marco Polo, to whom in mockery they attached the surname Millione. And Christopher Columbus for the same reason was for a long time reckoned mad. And in Vicenza at Carnival the companies put on masks and told nonsense in imitation of Antonio Pigafetta, who in the year 1522 went over to the Indies with Magellan.

The Romans, masters of Egypt, continued this voyage, for Strabo too makes mention of the Indian tribute, which in his time passed through Coptos, a city of Egypt. And Solinus relates a fine particular: that under the rule of Claudius a freedman of Annius Plocamus, who was collector of customs on the Red Sea, was going to Arabia and, carried off by the force of the wind, made land after fifteen days on the island of Taprobane. There, after six months, having learned the language of the country and having been brought before the king, he afterwards told many things that he had seen and noted; notable among them was the astonishment of that king that in the Roman coinage, struck with different faces, he nevertheless observed the same and uniform weight.

Pliny relates the same things. On this I must say that I cannot see on what the astonishment of that barbarian was based, since among many Roman denarii with the Balance in hand I have found very few that were of the same weight (and I have weighed and handled more than one). But to our business.

Solinus, in confirmation of what we have said, records the voyage that began in his time at Alexandria for India; and of this description of Solinus some trace is still seen in the ancient Itinerary Table published by Abraham Ortelius at the request of the most noble Signor Marcus Welser, a gentleman of the rarest qualities, to whom men of letters owe more than this alone. Arrian, nevertheless, denies that anyone ever came to discover the Ocean completely by the route of the Red Sea; but I believe him little, having on my side the testimonies written above, all the more because he confines himself to the times of Ptolemy the First, son of Lagus, and of Alexander the Great. He concedes, however, that Hanno the Carthaginian dared to pass the Pillars of Hercules and sailed for thirty-five days toward the east, but that, turning to the south, overcome by thirst and heat, he returned back.

Now whether the Egyptians had knowledge of the West Indies or not, there is much to doubt; nevertheless Benito Arias Montano, in his *Apparatus to the Royal Bible*, holds that the land of Ophir named in the Books of Kings and in the Paralipomena was Peru and New Spain; and perhaps he is not far from the truth; for if the Hebrews and those of Tyre [?] had knowledge of it, it would be nonsense to say that the Egyptians did not have it, since Solomon's fleet for that voyage was fitted out, as the Scripture says, in the port of Ezion-geber, near Ailath, on the shore of the Red Sea, which may be said to be in the Egyptians' house.
qm: "que' di Tito": probably a misprint for *Tiro* (the Tyrians, in Solomon's time); rendered "those of Tyre" with [?].

blocks.text: I know well that Gaspar Barreiros, a Portuguese, and Cornelis Wytfliet of Louvain have tried to prove that the land of Ophir was Malacca; but I also know that Abraham Ortelius, a man of that exquisite knowledge of geographical matters which the world knows, has embraced the opinion of Arias Montano and rejected that of Barreiros, and with Ortelius other authors also hold. But leaving authorities aside, I wish to avail myself on this point of a conjecture not at all weak, and it is that the peoples of this part of the world have conformed so closely, in the making of their idols, to the images of the Egyptian deities that they could not be more alike.

And I reason that before the Egyptians the inhabitants of these countries worshipped the Sun and the Moon and the host of heaven, as the Scripture says, which was the most ancient kind of idolatry ever seen in the world; and of this the memory was still kept here, nor had their successors forgotten it, but rather had formed from it a mixture that lasted until the introduction of the Gospel. But to give some beginning to this curious discourse, I shall give here the portrait of Homoyoca, god of Mexico, who among that wretched paganism was their Jupiter.

This meant in that language as much as the Creator of the whole, or the first cause, and they also called him Hometeutle, as if lord of three dignities, or lord three, Eli olomies. They called the dwelling of this god of theirs Narihnepaniuhca, which meant above the nine compositions, or by another name Homeiocam, that is, place of the triune lord. And he, according to the opinion of their wise men, begot with the word Cipatoual, and a woman called Xumoco, who are the two that were before the Flood, and who afterwards begot Tocatiutle. And from this it is plainly seen how true is what St Paul writes, that the invisible things of God are understood by man quite often by means of those that are seen; since in the midst of this barbarism there still shone a little light of nine higher causes, which we call heavens, and, besides, of the first cause, in which they obscurely foreshadowed, in their own way, the ineffable mystery of the Most Holy Trinity.

Now as for this Homoyoca, in his garments and in his posture I should say that he was taken little less than bodily from the Egyptians, among whom Osiris was figured in such a manner, as can be seen, and as I noted already on the most ancient Isiac Table of His Most Serene Highness the Duke of Mantua, on whose border a similar image is seen seventeen times, varied, however, in the ornaments.

Another image of Homopoca [?], or of a similar deity, has come into my hands, which, however, others call that of Quetzalcoatl.
